docs.title: 2. Actions, Routing, Responses
docs.text: This chapter examines the path a request takes, from the browser to the action that processes it, and the response that action returns. Views will not be introduced until Chapter 4: here, actions return text or JSON directly.

docs.title: 2.1. Example 01: The Structure of a Flask Application
docs.text:
The first example is the smallest possible [Flask] application: a single file.

01-structure/
└── app.py

docs.title: 2.1.1. The file app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the smallest possible Flask application
from flask import Flask

# the application: an instance of the Flask class. __name__ (here "__main__" or "app")
# tells Flask where the application is located so it can look for its files there
app = Flask(__name__)


# an action (Flask calls this a “view”): the function called for the request GET /
@app.get("/")
def index():
     # the value returned by the function EST the response sent to the browser
    return "Bonjour de la part de Flask !"


# executed only when the file itself is run: python app.py
if __name__ == "__main__":
     # the development server: http://localhost:5000; Ctrl-C stops it.
     # debug=True: automatic reload after a change, and
     # debug page in case of an error (JAMAIS in production)
    app.run(port=5000, debug=True)

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 2: imports the [Flask] class from the [flask] package, installed in the virtual environment by [pip]. In [Python], a file named [.py] is a module, and a module uses only the names it has imported or defined itself (aside from built-in language functions, such as [print] or [len]);
  • Line 6: the application, an object of the [Flask] class. It receives requests and selects the function that processes each one. The parameter is the name of the current module, which [Python] stores in the variable [__name__]: [Flask] uses this to locate the application folder, where it will later search for the views (folder [templates]) and the static files (folder [static]);
  • Line 10: [@app.get("/")] is a decorator. A decorator is written as [@expression], immediately before the definition of a function (or a class); [Python] calls the expression with the function as a parameter when it executes the definition. Here, [app.get("/")] registers the function [index] in the application: it will handle requests for [GET /]. This is routing. A function associated with a route in this way is an action (the [Flask] documentation refers to it as a view function; see the introduction);
  • lines 11–13: the action returns a string. The value returned by an action is the response sent to the browser: [Flask] places it in the body of the HTTP response. By convention, function names ([Python]) are written in lowercase, with words separated by underscores ([action01_post]);
  • line 17: when the file itself is executed ([python app.py]), [Python] assigns the value ["__main__"] to the variable [__name__]; when the module is imported by another module, it is set to the module’s name (["app"]). This test, which is very common in [Python], therefore reserves the rest of the code for when the file is launched directly;
  • line 21: [app.run] starts the [Werkzeug] development server, which listens for requests on port 5000 of the machine (5000 is the default value) until it is stopped by [Ctrl-C]. [debug=True] enables debug mode: the server monitors the application files and restarts the application as soon as one is modified; an unhandled exception displays a debug page (see Example 03). This mode is intended for development, and development only: the debug page allows you to execute [Python] code on the server.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Execution
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [01-structure] folder, with the examples’ virtual environment enabled, type [python app.py]. [Flask] displays its startup messages:

 * Serving Flask app 'app'
 * Debug mode: on
WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment. Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000
Press CTRL+C to quit
 * Restarting with stat
 * Debugger is active!
 * Debugger PIN: 332-612-699

The messages show the application name, debug mode, listening address, and port. [127.0.0.1] is the address of the machine itself ([localhost]): the server accepts only requests from this machine, which is suitable for development ([app.run(host="0.0.0.0")] would open it up to other machines on the network). The line [Restarting with stat] indicates the automatic reload mechanism: the process launched by [python app.py] simply monitors the files; it launches the application in a separate process, which it restarts whenever a change is made. "PIN" protects the [Python] console from the debug page.

There is a second way to launch an application: the [flask] command, installed along with [Flask] in the virtual environment:

flask --app app run --debug

The option [--app] specifies the application module ([app], i.e., the file [app.py]), [run] starts the development server, and [--debug] enables debug mode; [--port 5001] would change the port. The command itself locates, within the module, the object [Flask] named [app] (or, as we’ll see in Example 02, a function named [create_app]). With this, the [if __name__ == "__main__"] test is no longer needed. The examples use [python app.py], which is easier to remember; the case study will do the same.

Let’s request URL and [http://localhost:5000/] using a browser:

then with [curl]. The [-i] option also displays the HTTP headers from the response:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: Werkzeug/3.1.8 Python/3.13.7
Date: Sat, 26 Sep 2026 13:22:44 GMT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 29
Connection: close

Bonjour de la part de Flask !

The first line of the response contains the protocol version, the status code (200), and its label ([OK]). This is followed by the headers: the server name, the date, the content type, the content length in bytes, and [Connection: close] (the development server closes the connection after each response). A blank line separates the headers from the body of the response. In the rest of this document, we will no longer include the headers [Server], [Date], and [Connection], as they do not change.

The header [Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8] indicates that the response is in the format HTML, whose characters are encoded in UTF-8. This is the default encoding ([Flask]) for any string returned by an action: the browser therefore interprets the string as HTML (here, without a tag, it is displayed as-is). Example 03 will show how to specify a different encoding type.

For each request, the server console displays a log line: the client’s address, the date, the request, and the response code.

127.0.0.1 - - [26/Sep/2026 15:22:44] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -

docs.title: 2.2. Example 02: Routing
docs.text:
Routing associates a URL and a method (HTTP, GET, POST...) with an action. Example 02 organizes these actions into two files:

02-routage/
├── controllers/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── accueil.py
│   └── premier.py
└── app.py

The [controllers] folder is a [Python] package (see introduction). Each of these two modules defines a blueprint: a group of routes, which the application then registers. This is the [Flask] equivalent of the controller classes in [Spring MVC] or [ASP.NET Core MVC].

docs.title: 2.2.1. The application: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application, built by a "factory"
from flask import Flask

from controllers.accueil import accueil
from controllers.premier import premier


# the factory: a function that builds and configures the application
def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
     # Each blueprint (a group of routes) is registered with the application
    app.register_blueprint(accueil)
    app.register_blueprint(premier)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 4–5: Import the two blueprints, the objects [accueil] and [premier], from the modules [controllers/accueil.py] and [controllers/premier.py];
  • Lines 9–14: The application is no longer a module variable created upon import; it is constructed by a function called a *factory*. This is the approach recommended by the [Flask] documentation, which all subsequent examples will follow: the application’s configuration is consolidated in a single location, and multiple applications with different configurations can be created (for testing, for example). The [flask --app app run] command recognizes this: in the absence of a [app] variable, it calls the [create_app] function from the module;
  • lines 12–13: Each blueprint is registered in the application; its routes become those of the application;
  • line 18: the application is built, then the server is started.

docs.title: 2.2.2. The "home" blueprint: controllers/accueil.py
docs.text:
# controllers/accueil.py: the home page
from flask import Blueprint

# A blueprint: a set of routes, which is then registered with the application.
# "home": its name; __name__: the module where it is defined
accueil = Blueprint("accueil", __name__)


# GET /: a page (HTML) that contains links to other actions.
# A string returned by an action is sent with the text/html type
@accueil.get("/")
def index():
    return """
        <h2>Exemple 02 - le routage</h2>
        <ul>
          <li><a href="/premier">/premier</a></li>
          <li><a href="/premier/action01">/premier/action01</a></li>
          <li><a href="/premier/produits/17">/premier/produits/17</a></li>
          <li><a href="/premier/produits/17/avis/3">/premier/produits/17/avis/3</a></li>
          <li><a href="/premier/fichiers/images/logo.png">/premier/fichiers/images/logo.png</a></li>
          <li><a href="/premier/produits/abc">/premier/produits/abc</a></li>
          <li><a href="/inconnue">/inconnue</a></li>
        </ul>
        """
  • line 6: the blueprint. Its first parameter is its name, [accueil]: this will be used to identify its actions ([accueil.index], see Example 04). The second parameter, as with the application, is the module name;
  • line 11: A blueprint has the same decorators as the application: the action [index] processes [GET /];
  • lines 13–23: A string enclosed in triple quotes can span multiple lines and contain quotes. The action returns HTML, sent with the type [text/html] (see Example 01).

The action [index] thus returns a page HTML that contains links to the actions in the other blueprint:

docs.title: 2.2.3. The first blueprint: controllers/premier.py
docs.text:
# controllers/premier.py: a blueprint in which all routes begin with /premier
from flask import Blueprint

# url_prefix: a prefix common to all routes in the blueprint
premier = Blueprint("premier", __name__, url_prefix="/premier")


# GET /premier: the route "" refers to the prefix itself
@premier.get("")
def index():
    return "Action [index] du blueprint [premier]"


# GET /first/action01
@premier.get("/action01")
def action01():
    return "Action [action01] du blueprint [premier], requête GET"


# POST /first/action01: same path, different method HTTP, different function
@premier.post("/action01")
def action01_post():
    return "Action [action01_post] du blueprint [premier], requête POST"


# GET /first/products/17: <int:id> is a path variable;
# the [int] converter accepts only digits and returns an integer
@premier.get("/produits/<int:id>")
def produit(id):
    return f"Produit n° {id}"


# GET /first/products/17/reviews/3: two path variables
@premier.get("/produits/<int:id>/avis/<int:numero>")
def avis(id, numero):
    return f"Avis n° {numero} du produit n° {id}"


# GET /first/files/... : the [path] converter accepts any
# path ending, including slashes
@premier.get("/fichiers/<path:chemin>")
def fichier(chemin):
    return f"Fichier demandé : {chemin}"

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 5: the parameter [url_prefix] sets the prefix common to all routes in the blueprint: its actions handle URL routes that begin with [/premier];
  • Lines 9–10: The route [""] refers to the prefix itself: the action [index] handles [GET /premier]. The URL of an action is the concatenation of the blueprint’s prefix and the path of its route. The action name ([index]) may be the same as in another blueprint: [Flask] distinguishes them by the blueprint name ([premier.index], [accueil.index]);
  • lines 15–16: the action [action01] processes [GET /premier/action01];
  • lines 21–22: the same path, but for the method POST: the decorator [post] replaces [get]. There are also [put], [delete], and [patch], as well as the general decorator [route], which accepts a list of methods: [@premier.route("/action01", methods=["GET", "POST"])]. Within the same module, two functions cannot have the same name (the second would replace the first): hence the name [action01_post];
  • Lines 28–30: [<int:id>] is a path variable: this segment of URL can take on multiple values. [int] is a converter: the segment must consist of digits; otherwise, the route does not match; its value is converted to an integer and then passed to the action’s parameter of the same name, [id]. For [/premier/produits/17], [id] is equal to the number 17. This is data binding (*data binding*), which the next chapter will examine in detail. Without a converter ([<id>]), the variable accepts any text without a slash and remains a string. [Werkzeug] also provides the converters [float], [uuid], and [path], and Example 12 will show how to write your own;
  • Line 30: an f-string (the prefix [f]): each expression within curly braces is evaluated, and its value is inserted into the text;
  • lines 34–36: two path variables, passed as two parameters to the action;
  • lines 41–43: the [path] converter accepts any ending of URL, including [/].

docs.title: 2.2.4. Execution
docs.text:
Here are the responses to a few queries:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/first

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 37

Action [index] du blueprint [premier]

curl -i http://localhost:5000/first/products/17/reviews/3

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 28

Avis n° 3 du produit n° 17

The text is 26 characters long, but the response is 28 bytes: in UTF-8, the character [°] takes up two bytes.

curl -i http://localhost:5000/first/files/images/logo.png

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 34

Fichier demandé : images/logo.png

To send a request for POST, use the [-X POST] option of [curl]:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5000/first/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 60

Action [action01_post] du blueprint [premier], requête POST

A HTTP method that is not handled by any action for this path results in a 405 error ([Method Not Allowed]). The [Allow] header lists the accepted methods; [Flask] adds [HEAD] (the same request as GET, without the response body) and [OPTIONS] (the list of accepted methods), which it processes itself for any route GET:

curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:5000/first/action01

HTTP/1.1 405 METHOD NOT ALLOWED
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Allow: OPTIONS, POST, GET, HEAD
Content-Length: 153

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>405 Method Not Allowed</title>
<h1>Method Not Allowed</h1>
<p>The method is not allowed for the requested URL.</p>

Finally, a URL that no route handles results in a 404 error. This is also the case for an identifier that is not an integer: no route matches [/premier/produits/abc].

curl -i http://localhost:5000/first/products/abc

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 207

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>404 Not Found</title>
<h1>Not Found</h1>
<p>The requested URL was not found on the server. If you entered the URL manually please check your spelling and try again.</p>

The error responses for [Flask] (actually, for [Werkzeug]) are short pages named HTML, in English. In a browser:

Chapter 7 will show how to replace them with application-specific pages. Note also that [Flask] distinguishes [/premier] from [/premier/]: the latter, URL, also produces a 404 error, because no route ends with a forward slash. Conversely, a route declared with a trailing slash ([@premier.get("/liste/")]) also accepts URL without a slash, via a redirect.

The command [flask routes], run in the example folder, lists all the routes in the application:

flask --app app routes

Endpoint               Methods  Rule
---------------------  -------  --------------------------------------------
accueil.index          GET      /
premier.action01       GET      /premier/action01
premier.action01_post  POST     /premier/action01
premier.avis           GET      /premier/produits/<int:id>/avis/<int:numero>
premier.fichier        GET      /premier/fichiers/<path:chemin>
premier.index          GET      /premier
premier.produit        GET      /premier/produits/<int:id>
static                 GET      /static/<path:filename>

The [Endpoint] column lists the name of each route: the blueprint name, a period, and the function name. The last route, [static], is created by [Flask] itself: it serves the files in the application’s [static] folder (see Example 15).

docs.title: 2.3. Example 03: Responses from an action
docs.text:
What an action returns determines the response HTTP. Example 03 reviews the main cases. The file [app.py]:

# app.py: the application from Example 03
from flask import Flask

from controllers.reponses import reponses


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
     # The JSON output preserves accented characters as-is ("créée" rather than
     # "cr\u00e9\u00e9e"), and the keys in their original order (not sorted)
    app.json.ensure_ascii = False
    app.json.sort_keys = False
    app.register_blueprint(reponses)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 11–12: two settings for the application’s JSON provider ([app.json]), the object that converts [Python] objects to JSON. By default, it writes non-ASCII characters as escape sequences ([créée] becomes [créée], which is valid JSON but not very readable), and it sorts dictionary keys alphabetically. We keep the characters as-is, and the keys in the order in which the action wrote them.

The file [controllers/reponses.py]:

# controllers/reponses.py: the various responses to an action
import asyncio
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

from flask import Blueprint, Response, abort, jsonify

reponses = Blueprint("reponses", __name__, url_prefix="/reponses")


# a string, declared as plain text: the browser displays it as-is.
# Response: the complete response, constructed by the action itself
@reponses.get("/texte")
def texte():
    return Response("<h1>Action [texte]</h1>", mimetype="text/plain")


# a single string: Flask sends it with the text/html MIME type; the browser interprets it
@reponses.get("/html")
def html():
    return "<h1>Action [html]</h1>"


# a dataclass: a data class (see Example 06), declared here in the module
@dataclass
class Personne:
    nom: str
    prenom: str
    age: int


# an object: `jsonify` serializes it to `JSON`, with the type `[application/json]`
@reponses.get("/json")
def json():
    return jsonify(Personne("Martin", "Jean", 42))


# a dictionary rendered as-is: Flask serializes it itself into JSON
@reponses.get("/dictionnaire")
def dictionnaire():
    return {"nom": "Martin", "prenom": "Jean", "age": 42}


# a list: serialized as an array JSON
@reponses.get("/liste")
def liste():
    return ["Mme", "Melle", "Mr"]


# a tuple (content, status code): status code 201 (Created) instead of 200 (OK)
@reponses.get("/cree")
def cree():
    return {"message": "ressource créée"}, 201


# no response: status code 204 (No Content) means “nothing to display”
@reponses.get("/vide")
def vide():
    return "", 204


# an asynchronous action (async def): Flask waits for the coroutine to finish.
# You need the Flask extension [async]: pip install "flask[async]"
@reponses.get("/tache")
async def tache():
    debut = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)  # A 500 ms wait, without blocking the event loop
    return {"attente": f"{round((time.perf_counter() - debut) * 1000)} ms"}


# An "expected" error: the tuple (content, 404) produces a 404 response
@reponses.get("/introuvable")
def introuvable():
    return {"message": "Cette ressource n'existe pas"}, 404


# the same, via abort: a HTTP exception, which Flask converts to a 404 response
@reponses.get("/abandon")
def abandon():
    abort(404, "Cette ressource n'existe pas non plus")


# an "unexpected" error: an unhandled exception results in a 500 response
@reponses.get("/exception")
def exception():
    raise RuntimeError("Une erreur imprévue")

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 13–15: The class [Response] represents a complete HTTP response. The action constructs it itself: the body and the type ([mimetype]), in this case [text/plain] (plain text). The browser will not interpret the tags;
  • lines 19–21: the same string, rendered on its own: [Flask] sends it with the type [text/html], and the browser interprets it;
  • lines 25–29: a dataclass—a class in which only the fields and their types are declared; the decorator [@dataclass] writes the constructor ([Personne("Martin", "Jean", 42)]), the textual representation, and the object comparison itself. Example 06 will revisit this;
  • lines 33–35: the function [jsonify] converts its parameter to JSON and generates a response of type [application/json]. The provider JSON for [Flask] can convert dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, Booleans, [None] (which becomes [null]), as well as dataclasses, dates, and numbers [Decimal] (see example 06);
  • lines 39–41: even simpler: an action that returns a dictionary (or a list, lines 45–47) produces a response JSON, without calling [jsonify]. A dataclass, on the other hand, must go through [jsonify]: if returned on its own, it would cause an error (“The view function did not return a valid response”);
  • lines 51–53: An action can return a tuple [(contenu, code)]: status code 201 ([Created]) replaces status code 200. A tuple can also contain headers: [(contenu, code, {"X-Exemple": "03"})];
  • lines 57–59: code 204 ([No Content]) means “nothing to display”: the response has no body;
  • lines 64–68: an asynchronous action, declared by [async def]. The keyword [await] suspends the coroutine while waiting ([asyncio.sleep]), without blocking the program. [Flask] executes the action in an event loop created for the request and waits for its result: this is useful for launching multiple waits in parallel (multiple calls to web services, for example), but it does not make [Flask] itself asynchronous. You must install the [[async]] extension of [Flask] (see [requirements.txt]);
  • lines 72–74: an “expected” error: the tuple [(contenu, 404)] returns a 404 response ([Not Found]), with a body (JSON) chosen by the action;
  • lines 78–80: the same error, generated by the function [abort]. [abort] returns nothing: it throws an exception ([NotFound], for the 404 code), which terminates the action; [Flask] converts it into an error response, with the message provided as the second parameter. This is the most common way to terminate an action due to an error, even deep within a function called by the action;
  • lines 84–86: an “unexpected” error—an exception that no one handles—produces a 500 response ([Internal Server Error]).

In a browser, the difference between [text/plain] and [text/html] is visible:

Here are the responses for the other actions:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 55

{
  "nom": "Martin",
  "prenom": "Jean",
  "age": 42
}

The dataclass has been converted to the object JSON, with one field per attribute. In debug mode, JSON is displayed on multiple lines, indented; without debug mode, it fits on a single line ([{"nom":"Martin","prenom":"Jean","age":42}]). The action [/reponses/dictionnaire] produces exactly the same output.

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/list

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 31

[
  "Mme",
  "Melle",
  "Mr"
]

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/create

HTTP/1.1 201 CREATED
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 37

{
  "message": "ressource créée"
}

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/empty

HTTP/1.1 204 NO CONTENT
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/task

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 26

{
  "attente": "501 ms"
}

curl -i http://localhost:5000/responses/not-found

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 48

{
  "message": "Cette ressource n'existe pas"
}

curl -i http://localhost:5000/answers/abandoned

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 128

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>404 Not Found</title>
<h1>Not Found</h1>
<p>Cette ressource n'does not exist either</p>

The response from [abort] is the standard error page for [Werkzeug], with our message (its apostrophe was escaped in [']: text inserted into HTML must not be able to introduce tags there; we’ll come back to this).

That leaves the unhandled exception. In debug mode, the browser displays the [Werkzeug] debugger page: the exception type and message, followed by the call stack (the list of functions that were executing at the time of the error), from oldest to most recent, with the relevant line of code for each:

The last function in the stack is our action, [exception], on line 86 of the file [reponses.py]. By clicking on one of the lines in the stack, you can even open a [Python] console in the context of that function, after entering the PIN displayed at startup: this is why debug mode should never be enabled on a server accessible to others. The server console also displays the call stack (we’ve included only the end here):

127.0.0.1 - - [26/Sep/2026 15:23:10] "GET /reponses/exception HTTP/1.1" 500 -
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../exemples/03-reponses/controllers/reponses.py", line 86, in exception
    raise RuntimeError("Une erreur imprévue")
RuntimeError: Une erreur imprévue

Without debug mode ([app.run(port=5000)]), the same request produces a brief 500 error page in English that reveals nothing about the code (“Internal Server Error. The server encountered an internal error and was unable to complete your request...”); the call stack is only written to the server console. Chapter 7 will show how to display an application-specific error page.

docs.title: 2.4. Example 04: Redirects
docs.text:
A redirect is a response that instructs the browser to fetch another URL: a 3xx code and the [Location] header, which contains the new address. The browser immediately sends a second request to that address. The [controllers/redirections.py] file:

# controllers/redirections.py: redirects
from flask import Blueprint, redirect, url_for

redirections = Blueprint("redirections", __name__)


# permanent redirect (301): the page has permanently changed its address
@redirections.get("/ancienne")
def ancienne():
    return redirect("/nouvelle", code=301)


@redirections.get("/nouvelle")
def nouvelle():
    return "Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]"


# temporary redirect (302, the default code), to a calculated address
# by piecing together text segments
@redirections.get("/aller/<destination>")
def aller(destination):
    return redirect("/page/" + destination)


# url_for generates the address of a ACTION, identified by its name
# ("blueprint.fonction"): the parameter [nom] is correctly encoded for a URL
@redirections.get("/vers-modele/<destination>")
def vers_modele(destination):
    return redirect(url_for("redirections.page", nom=destination))


@redirections.get("/page/<nom>")
def page(nom):
    return f"Vous êtes sur la page [{nom}]"


# redirect to another site
@redirections.get("/documentation")
def documentation():
    return redirect("https://flask.palletsprojects.com/")
  • lines 8–10: The [redirect] function generates a redirect response to the specified address. The 301 status code ([Moved Permanently]) indicates that the page has permanently changed its address: the browser (and search engines) can cache the new one;
  • lines 20–22: Without the [code] parameter, [redirect] produces a temporary redirect with a 302 status code ([Found]). The address is calculated by concatenating pieces of text, which poses a problem that we will examine;
  • Lines 27–29: The function [url_for] generates the URL for an action, identified by its name (["redirections.page"]: the blueprint, a point, the function), rather than by its path. Its named parameters provide the path variables (here, [nom]), correctly encoded for a URL. If the path of the route [page] is ever changed, calls to [url_for] will automatically follow suit;
  • lines 38–40: a redirect to another site.

The responses, using [curl] (which, without any options, does not follow redirects):

curl -i http://localhost:5000/old

HTTP/1.1 301 MOVED PERMANENTLY
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 205
Location: /nouvelle

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>Redirecting...</title>
<h1>Redirecting...</h1>
<p>You should be redirected automatically to the target URL: <a href="/nouvelle">/nouvelle</a>. If not, click the link.

The response also includes a small body, HTML, for a client that would not follow redirects. The [-L] option of [curl] follows the redirect, just as a browser would:

curl -L http://localhost:5000/old

Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]

Now let’s compare the two calculated redirects, with a destination that contains a question mark, encoded as [%3F] in URL (an uncoded [?] would start the parameters of the URL):

curl -i http://localhost:5000/go/a%3Fb

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 205
Location: /page/a?b

curl -i http://localhost:5000/to-template/a%3Fb

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 209
Location: /page/a%3Fb

[Flask] decoded the path variable before processing it: [destination] equals [a?b]. The first action pastes it as-is into the address: [/page/a?b], which the browser interprets as the path [/page/a] followed by the parameter [b]. The second one goes through [url_for], which encodes it again: [/page/a%3Fb]. Following the redirects:

curl -L http://localhost:5000/go/a%3Fb
curl -L http://localhost:5000/to-template/a%3Fb

Vous êtes sur la page [a]
Vous êtes sur la page [a?b]

Only the second one leads to the correct page. Hence the rule: an address containing a variable value is generated using [url_for], never by concatenating strings. In the browser, only the final page is visible; the address bar displays the new URL:

Two other redirect codes exist: 303 ([See Other]) and 307 ([Temporary Redirect]), which are obtained via [redirect(url, code=303)]. After a POST request, codes 302 and 303 cause the browser to send a GET request to the new address, whereas 307 (and 308, the permanent version) cause it to repeat the POST request. Example 20 will use redirection following a POST.

docs.title: 2.5. Example 05: The Request and Response Objects
docs.text:
Until now, actions only received path variables and returned a value that [Flask] converted into a response. An action can also access the current request and construct the response itself. The file [controllers/http.py]:

# controllers/http.py: the request and response objects
import time

from flask import Blueprint, Response, make_response, request

http = Blueprint("http", __name__, url_prefix="/http")


# The request: method, path, parameters, headers...
# [request] is a global Flask object that represents the request EN COURS
@http.get("/requete")
def requete():
     # A Python dictionary preserves the order in which its keys are inserted
    return {
        "methode": request.method,
        "chemin": request.path,
         # query_string: bytes, which are decoded into text
        "parametres": request.query_string.decode(),
        "navigateur": request.headers.get("User-Agent"),
        "ip": request.remote_addr,
    }


# the response: make_response constructs the response object from what
# the action would return; a header is added to it before it is returned
@http.get("/entete")
def entete():
    reponse = make_response("Réponse avec un entête ajouté")
    reponse.headers["X-Exemple"] = "05-requete-reponse"
    return reponse


# the “hand-built” response: body, code, type
@http.get("/reponse")
def reponse():
    return Response("Réponse construite par [Response(...)]", status=200,
                    mimetype="text/plain")


# a response sent PAR MORCEAUX: the code and headers are sent with the
# first chunk, and cannot be changed afterward
@http.get("/flux")
def flux():
    def morceaux():
        yield "Début de la réponse... "
        time.sleep(1)
         # too late to report an error: the 200 status code has already been sent
        raise RuntimeError("erreur au milieu de la réponse")

    return Response(morceaux(), mimetype="text/plain")
  • Line 4: Importing the [request] object. In [Flask], the current request is not a parameter of the action: it is a global object, [request], which is imported from the [flask] package. How can a global object refer to the current request, given that the server processes multiple requests simultaneously across multiple threads (parallel execution threads)? [request] acts as a proxy: each time it is used, it forwards the operation to the request in the current thread. [Flask] refers to this as the request context: while a request is being processed, [request] refers to that specific request. Outside of request processing, using it causes an error (“Working outside of request context”);
  • lines 14–20: some properties of the request: its method HTTP, its path, its raw parameters (the part of URL that follows [?], in byte form, which [decode] converts to text), its headers ([request.headers], a dictionary, whose method [get] returns [None] for a missing header), the client’s address IP. The parameters, one by one, will be covered in the next chapter;
  • lines 26–30: the function [make_response] constructs the response object (a [Response]) based on what the action would return (here, a string); the action can then modify it before returning it. A [X-Exemple] header is added to it (by convention, application-specific headers often begin with [X-]);
  • lines 34–37: the “hand-built” response: the body, the status code, and the type;
  • lines 42–50: a response sent in chunks (*streaming*). The function [morceaux] is a generator: each [yield] produces a chunk of the body. Since the response is built using a generator, its length is not known in advance: the server sends the status code and headers, then each chunk as soon as it is produced. This is useful for a very long response, generated bit by bit. But once the first chunk has been sent, the status code can no longer change: here, the generator throws an exception after the first chunk. This is the mistake to avoid: a response that has already begun cannot become an error response.

Responses:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/http/requete?nom=martin&age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 140

{
  "methode": "GET",
  "chemin": "/http/requete",
  "parametres": "nom=martin&age=42",
  "navigateur": "curl/8.5.0",
  "ip": "127.0.0.1"
}

(The quotation marks around "URL" prevent the terminal from interpreting the character "[&]".) In a browser, the [User-Agent] header is the browser's header; [Chrome] displays the raw JSON, with a checkbox that indents it:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/http/header

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 32
X-Exemple: 05-requete-reponse

Réponse avec un entête ajouté

curl -i http://localhost:5000/http/response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 39

Réponse construite par [Response(...)]

curl -i http://localhost:5000/http/feed

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

Début de la réponse...

The header [Transfer-Encoding: chunked] replaces [Content-Length]: the body arrives in chunks, each preceded by its length. After one second, the response stops: [curl] received a 200 status code and a truncated body, with no way of knowing that an error occurred. Only the server console indicates this:

Error on request:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../exemples/05-requete-reponse/controllers/http.py", line 48, in morceaux
    raise RuntimeError("erreur au milieu de la réponse")
RuntimeError: erreur au milieu de la réponse

docs.title: 2.6. Example 06: Shared Services and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
An action should not contain the application logic itself; it delegates it to services—objects that know how to perform a specific task (read products, calculate a shopping cart, etc.). Multiple actions often use the same service. In [Spring] or [ASP.NET Core], a dependency injection container creates the services and automatically provides them to those that need them. [Flask] does not have a container: the application factory creates the services, and the actions request them from the application. Example 06 organizes its code by domain (products, customers) rather than by type (controllers, models):

06-services/
├── clients/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── controller.py
├── produits/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── controller.py
│   ├── produit.py
│   ├── service.py
│   └── service_memoire.py
└── app.py

docs.title: 2.6.1. The Product
docs.text:
# products/produit.py: a product
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal


# a dataclass: Python writes the constructor itself, __repr__, __eq__...
# frozen=True: the object is immutable (its fields are set by the constructor)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Produit:
    id: int
    nom: str
    prix: Decimal  # Decimal: an exact decimal number (no binary rounding)
  • Line 8: a dataclass (see Example 03). With [frozen=True], the object is immutable: its fields are set by the constructor, and any attempt to modify them ([p.prix = 2]) throws an exception. An immutable object can be safely shared across multiple requests;
  • Lines 10–12: the fields, along with their types. Types are not checked by [Python] at runtime: they are annotations read by analysis tools (such as the one in [Visual Studio Code]) and certain libraries ([Pydantic], discussed in the next chapter). The price is a [Decimal], an exact decimal number: a [float] cannot accurately represent 0.1 or 3.2 (in binary, these numbers have an infinite number of digits), and a sum of prices in [float] may result in 5.500000000000001.

docs.title: 2.6.2. The service contract: service.py
docs.text:
# products/service.py: the service’s CONTRAT—what it can do, without specifying how
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

from flask import current_app

from produits.produit import Produit


# an abstract class (ABC): you cannot create an object of it; a class
# A child class must implement (override) all methods marked @abstractmethod
class ProduitsService(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def find_all(self) -> list[Produit]: ...

     # Product | None: a product, or None if it does not exist
    @abstractmethod
    def find_by_id(self, id: int) -> Produit | None: ...


# the service of the current application (see app.py). current_app refers to
# the application processing the current request
def produits_service() -> ProduitsService:
    return current_app.extensions["produits_service"]
  • Lines 11–18: the service contract—what it can do, without specifying how. In [Python], a contract is defined by an abstract class: a class that inherits from [ABC] ([Abstract Base Class]), and whose methods marked [@abstractmethod] have no body (the three dots [...] serve as an empty body). You cannot create an object of this class; a subclass must override all of its abstract methods. This is equivalent to the interfaces [Java] and [C#];
  • line 14: the annotation for the type returned by the method (after [->]): a list of products. [self] is the object on which the method is called (the equivalent of [this] in [Java]), always listed as the first parameter;
  • line 18: [Produit | None]: a product, or [None] if it does not exist;
  • Lines 23–24: The function that provides the service to the actions. [current_app] is, like [request], a proxy: it refers to the application that processes the current request. [app.extensions] is a dictionary that [Flask] makes available to extensions (the libraries that are added to [Flask]) so they can store their objects there; we use it for our own services. The function also specifies the service type ([-> ProduitsService]): [Visual Studio Code] can then offer its methods.

docs.title: 2.6.3. The implementation: service_memoire.py
docs.text:
# products/service_memoire.py: a IMPLÉMENTATION from the contract, with data in memory
from decimal import Decimal

from produits.produit import Produit
from produits.service import ProduitsService


class ProduitsServiceMemoire(ProduitsService):

    def __init__(self):
         # a tuple: a read-only list
        self._produits = (
            Produit(1, "stylo", Decimal("1.5")),
            Produit(2, "cahier", Decimal("3.2")),
            Produit(3, "gomme", Decimal("0.8")),
        )

    def find_all(self) -> list[Produit]:
        return list(self._produits)

    def find_by_id(self, id: int) -> Produit | None:
         # next(generator, None): the first matching product, or None
        return next((p for p in self._produits if p.id == id), None)
  • line 8: the class inherits the contract and redefines its two methods;
  • lines 10–15: [__init__] is the class’s constructor. It stores the products in the object’s [_produits] attribute; the leading underscore indicates, by convention, a private attribute that code outside the class should not use. The products are in a tuple (enclosed in parentheses): an immutable sequence. The price is constructed from a string ([Decimal("1.5")]): built from [float] 1.5, it would inherit its inaccuracies;
  • lines 18–19: The method returns a new list, a copy of the tuple: the caller can modify it without affecting the service’s data;
  • lines 21–23: [(p for p in self._produits if p.id == id)] is a generator expression: it produces, one by one, the products whose ID matches the requested one. [next] returns the first product element, or the default value, [None], if there are none.

docs.title: 2.6.4. The product blueprint: controller.py
docs.text:
# products/controller.py: actions from /products
from flask import Blueprint, jsonify

from produits.service import produits_service

produits = Blueprint("produits", __name__, url_prefix="/produits")


@produits.get("")
def liste():
     # the service is obtained from the application with each request
    return jsonify(produits_service().find_all())


@produits.get("/<int:id>")
def un_produit(id):
    produit = produits_service().find_by_id(id)
    if produit is None:
        return {"message": f"Produit n° {id} introuvable"}, 404
    return jsonify(produit)
  • Line 4: The blueprint knows only the service contract (the [service] module), not its implementation: it is unaware that the products are in memory;
  • Lines 10–12: The action requests the service from the application, then delegates the work to it. [jsonify] converts the list of dataclasses into an array JSON;
  • lines 16–20: an unknown product returns a 404 response, with a message in JSON.

docs.title: 2.6.5. The client blueprint: controller.py
docs.text:
# customers/controller.py: a second blueprint, which uses the MÊME service
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal

from flask import Blueprint, jsonify

from produits.service import produits_service

clients = Blueprint("clients", __name__, url_prefix="/clients")


# the contents of the shopping cart, rendered as JSON
@dataclass
class Panier:
    client: str
    articles: int
    total: Decimal


@clients.get("/panier")
def panier():
    produits = produits_service().find_all()
     # the sum of the prices; start=Decimal(0): Decimal values are added together
    total = sum((p.prix for p in produits), start=Decimal(0))
    return jsonify(Panier("Jean Martin", len(produits), total))
  • lines 14–17: the contents of the shopping cart, rendered as JSON;
  • line 22: this blueprint uses the same service as the products blueprint: a single, shared object;
  • line 24: [sum] sums the elements of an iterable; its parameter [start] is the initial value of the sum (0 by default). Starting with [Decimal(0)] rather than the integer 0 is not essential (an integer and a [Decimal] add together), but it guarantees a result of [Decimal] even for an empty shopping cart.

docs.title: 2.6.6. The service declaration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 06
from flask import Flask

from clients.controller import clients
from produits.controller import produits
from produits.service_memoire import ProduitsServiceMemoire


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
     # JSON: accents preserved, keys in their original order (see example 03)
    app.json.ensure_ascii = False
    app.json.sort_keys = False
     # SERVICE: a single object, created once at startup, and shared by
     # all requests. It is stored in app.extensions, a dictionary that
     # Flask makes available to extensions... and our services
    app.extensions["produits_service"] = ProduitsServiceMemoire()
    app.register_blueprint(produits)
    app.register_blueprint(clients)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Line 17: This is where—and only here—the service implementation is chosen. The service is created once, at startup, and the same object handles all requests from all users: it is a singleton (the default scope for [Spring] beans). To switch to an implementation that reads from a database, you would simply need to change this line: the blueprints, which only know the contract, would remain unchanged. This is the whole point of dependency injection, even when implemented “by hand”: every part of the application depends on contracts, and a single location determines the implementations.

A service shared by all requests must be able to handle being used simultaneously by multiple requests: the development server processes each request on its own thread. This poses no problem: it simply reads data that never changes. Example 20 will show a service whose data changes, and the precautions this requires.

docs.title: 2.6.7. Execution
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:5000/products

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 184

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "nom": "stylo",
    "prix": "1.5"
  },
  {
    "id": 2,
    "nom": "cahier",
    "prix": "3.2"
  },
  {
    "id": 3,
    "nom": "gomme",
    "prix": "0.8"
  }
]

The prices have become strings (["1.5"]): JSON has only a numeric type, which most programs interpret as a floating-point number; so the provider JSON for [Flask] converts a [Decimal] to a string to preserve its precision.

curl -i http://localhost:5000/products/9

HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 45

{
  "message": "Produit n° 9 introuvable"
}

curl -i http://localhost:5000/customers/cart

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 65

{
  "client": "Jean Martin",
  "articles": 3,
  "total": "5.5"
}

docs.title: 13.1. Installing Python
docs.text:
[Python] can be downloaded from python.org/downloads. The examples and case study require version 3.12 or later; they have been tested with version 3.13.

In [Windows], the installer displays the “Add python.exe to PATH” checkbox on its first screen: you must check it. The [python] command is then available in all terminals. The installer also installs the [py] launcher, which allows you to select a version when multiple versions are installed ([py -3.13]). You can also use the package manager [winget]:

winget install Python.Python.3.13

For [macOS], use the [.pkg] installer from the same page, or the [Homebrew] package manager ([brew install python@3.13]). Under [Linux], [Python] is usually already installed; check its version, and if necessary, install the [venv] module, which creates the virtual environments (under [Ubuntu]: [sudo apt install python3-venv]). Under [macOS] and [Linux], the command is often called [python3] (and [pip3]): this is the command used to create the virtual environment. Once the environment is activated, [python] and [pip] refer to those within the environment.

Verify the installation in a new console ([PowerShell], command prompt, or terminal):

python --version

which should display a version number equal to or greater than 3.12 (for example, [Python 3.13.7]). With an older version, the case study stops at startup due to a syntax error (see “Common Issues”).

docs.title: 13.2. Virtual Environments and pip
docs.text:
A virtual environment is a folder (in this case, [.venv]) that contains a copy of the [Python] interpreter and a project's libraries. Each project thus has its own, in the versions that suit it. The [exemples] folder has its own environment, shared by all 28 examples; the case study has its own.

Useful commands, under [Windows] (under [Linux] and [macOS], [source .venv/bin/activate] for activation):

python -m venv .venv               # Create the environment (once)
.venv\Scripts\activate             # Activate it (in each new terminal)
pip install -r requirements.txt    # install the project libraries
pip list                           # the installed libraries
deactivate                         # deactivate the environment

[pip] downloads the libraries from the repository [PyPI] (pypi.org): an Internet connection is required during installation. If you are behind a corporate proxy, specify the proxy using the [--proxy] option in [pip]. The virtual environment cannot be copied from one machine to another (it contains absolute paths): you must recreate it using the [requirements.txt] file. This is why the [.venv] folder is not included in the course materials.

docs.title: 13.3. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Download [Visual Studio Code] from code.visualstudio.com. Add the Microsoft Python extension (View menu / Extensions, then search for “Python”): this also installs [Pylance] (autocompletion, type checking, error reporting) and the Python Debugger. An extension like Better Jinja adds syntax highlighting to [Jinja2] views (HTML files containing {{ }} and {% %} tags).

Open the [exemples] folder or the case study folder (File menu / Open Folder). The extension detects the [.venv] virtual environment and prompts you to use it: accept the prompt (you can also select it using the Python command: Select Interpreter, [Ctrl-Maj-P] keys). The built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) then automatically activates the environment, allowing you to run applications without leaving the editor. The [F5] key, in the [app.py] file, runs the application under the debugger’s control (see “Development Mode”).

docs.title: 13.4. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] (laragon.org) installs a ready-to-use [MySQL] server (or [MariaDB]) ready for use, along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the "Start All" button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the default values from Example 28 ([DATABASE_URL]) and the case study ([DB_USER], [DB_PASSWORD]);
  • the Database button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File menu / Run File SQL runs the scripts [dbpersonnes.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

For [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system's package manager, and run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql]. The [PyMySQL] driver works with both without any configuration. Under [Linux], the [root] account for [MariaDB] is often configured to log in only via the system account [root] ([sudo mysql]): In this case, a user is created for the applications, and this user is specified in their configuration:

sudo mysql -e "CREATE USER 'cours'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'cours'; GRANT ALL ON *.* TO 'cours'@'localhost';"

docs.title: 13.5. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] is included with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. On [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options. In the command prompt for [Windows] ([cmd]), the quotation marks for a string JSON are written as [\"] (example 11), and a URL that contains [&] must be enclosed in double quotes.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and every subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Do they have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Since the server is stateless (see the chapter on scopes), proof of identity must be included with every request. A token named JWT (*JSON Web Token*) is used: After login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key. The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature. This is the same principle as the [Flask] session (Example 20), but with a standardized format (RFC 7519) that is understood by all programming languages, and an expiration date embedded in the token.

[Flask] does not have a built-in security mechanism, unlike [Spring] ([Spring Security]) or [ASP.NET Core]. Extensions exist ([Flask-Login], [Flask-JWT-Extended]...), but the mechanism is simple enough to be written by hand using the tools from the previous chapters, which has the advantage of making it transparent:

  • authentication is handled by a function [before_request] (previous chapter), which retrieves the token from the cookie, verifies it, and stores the authenticated user in [g], the request object;
  • authorization is handled by decorators applied to the actions ([@connexion_requise], [@role_requis("ADMIN")]), built like the [@avec_langue] decorator in Example 12.

Two libraries are used, installed by the [requirements.txt] file from the examples: [PyJWT], which generates and verifies tokens, and [bcrypt], which hashes passwords.

docs.title: 8.1.1. Configuration: config.py and app.py
docs.text:
The token is signed with a secret key, which must not be hard-coded. It’s time to separate the configuration from the code:

# config.py: the application configuration, read by app.config.from_pyfile.
# Only the variables in MAJUSCULES are retained.

# The key that signs the JWT tokens (at least 32 characters) and their lifetime
JWT_SECRET = "une-cle-secrete-d-au-moins-32-caracteres-pour-l-exemple-25"
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES = 60

A [Flask] configuration file is simply a [Python] module: its variables in uppercase become keys for [app.config]. [JWT_SECRET] is the token signing key; the standard requires, for the algorithm used (HMAC-SHA256), a key of at least 256 bits, or 32 bytes. [JWT_DUREE_MINUTES] is the lifetime of a token.

# app.py: the application from Example 25
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask

from auth import securite
from auth.service import AuthService
from auth.utilisateurs import UtilisateursService
from controllers.auth import auth
from controllers.profil import profil

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
     # the configuration: the file config.py, followed by the environment variables
     # that begin with FLASK_ (FLASK_JWT_SECRET replaces JWT_SECRET)
    app.config.from_pyfile("config.py")
    app.config.from_prefixed_env()
     # authentication services
    utilisateurs = UtilisateursService()
    app.extensions["auth"] = AuthService(utilisateurs, app.config["JWT_SECRET"],
                                         app.config["JWT_DUREE_MINUTES"])
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(auth)
    app.register_blueprint(profil)
     # the user for each request, read from the cookie token
    securite.enregistrer(app)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • line 21: reading the configuration file, specified by a path relative to the application folder;
  • line 22: reading environment variables whose names begin with [FLASK_]: [FLASK_JWT_SECRET] replaces the key [JWT_SECRET] in the file. The value of a variable is interpreted as JSON whenever possible ([FLASK_JWT_DUREE_MINUTES=30] yields the integer 30). In production, the secret key is provided by the environment, and the file contains only a development value;
  • lines 24–26: the two authentication services, the second of which receives the key and the token lifetime;
  • line 32: the registration of the [before_request] function, which reads the token.

Under [Linux] or [macOS], the application would be launched with a different key as follows:

FLASK_JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres" python app.py

and under [Windows] (PowerShell):

$env:FLASK_JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres"
python app.py

docs.title: 8.1.2. Users: auth/utilisateurs.py
docs.text:
# auth/utilisateurs.py: users, in memory (Example 28 and the case study
# will store them in a database)
from dataclasses import dataclass

import bcrypt


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Utilisateur:
    login: str
    nom: str
    role: str
    hachage_mot_de_passe: bytes


# password hashing: bcrypt, with a cost of 10 (2^10 rounds);
# gensalt generates a random “salt,” which is stored within the hash itself
def hacher(mot_de_passe: str) -> bytes:
    return bcrypt.hashpw(mot_de_passe.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=10))


class UtilisateursService:

    def __init__(self):
         # We do not store JAMAIS a password, only its hash
        self._utilisateurs = {u.login: u for u in (
            Utilisateur("marie", "Marie Pélissier", "USER", hacher("marie")),
            Utilisateur("admin", "Administrateur", "ADMIN", hacher("admin")),
        )}

    def chercher(self, login: str) -> Utilisateur | None:
        return self._utilisateurs.get(login)
  • Lines 9–13: a user: their login, name, role, and password hash. A server never stores a password, even in encrypted form: if the database were stolen, the passwords would be too (and many people use the same password everywhere). It stores the result of a hash function, a one-way function: you can calculate the hash of a password, but you cannot recover a password from its hash. To verify an entered password, you calculate its hash and compare it to the one on file;
  • lines 18–19: hashing using the [bcrypt] algorithm, designed for passwords. It has two distinctive features. It is intentionally slow, with an adjustable slowness (the parameter [rounds], or cost: 2^10 computation cycles): a few tens of milliseconds, imperceptible to a user, but which makes it very costly for a hacker to try billions of passwords. It uses a salt: [gensalt] randomly generates a salt, mixes it with the password before hashing, and stores it within the hash itself; thus, two users with the same password will have different hashes. [bcrypt] operates on bytes: [encode()] converts the string into bytes ([UTF-8]). It considers only the first 72 bytes of a password, and version 5 of the library rejects longer passwords (the case study takes this into account);
  • Lines 26–28: two test users, stored in memory, organized in a dictionary built during processing ([{clé: valeur for ...}]). Example 28 and the case study will store them in a database.

docs.title: 8.1.3. The authentication service: auth/service.py
docs.text:
# auth/service.py: password verification and tokens JWT
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import bcrypt
import jwt
from flask import current_app

from auth.utilisateurs import Utilisateur, UtilisateursService

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
COOKIE = "jeton"


class AuthService:

    def __init__(self, utilisateurs: UtilisateursService, secret: str, duree_minutes: int):
        self._utilisateurs = utilisateurs
        self._secret = secret
        self.duree = timedelta(minutes=duree_minutes)

     # the user, or None if the login is unknown or the password is incorrect.
     # checkpw hashes the entered password with the stored hash salt,
     # then compares the two results
    def valider(self, login: str | None, mot_de_passe: str | None) -> Utilisateur | None:
        if not login or mot_de_passe is None:
            return None
        utilisateur = self._utilisateurs.chercher(login)
        if utilisateur is None or not bcrypt.checkpw(mot_de_passe.encode(),
                                                     utilisateur.hachage_mot_de_passe):
            return None
        return utilisateur

     # the user’s token (JWT), signed with the secret key (HMAC-SHA256)
    def creer_jeton(self, utilisateur: Utilisateur) -> str:
        maintenant = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
         # the token’s content: the “claims” (statements about the user)
        claims = {
            "sub": utilisateur.login,
            "nom": utilisateur.nom,
            "role": utilisateur.role,
            "iat": maintenant,
            "exp": maintenant + self.duree,
        }
        return jwt.encode(claims, self._secret, algorithm="HS256")

     # the claims of a token whose signature and expiration date are
     # valid; None otherwise (token is forged, expired, or unreadable)
    def verifier(self, jeton: str) -> dict | None:
        try:
            return jwt.decode(jeton, self._secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
        except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
            return None


def auth_service() -> AuthService:
    return current_app.extensions["auth"]
  • Lines 24–31: Verification of a username and password. [bcrypt.checkpw] hashes the entered password using the stored hash salt and compares the two hashes. An unknown username and an incorrect password yield the same result, [None];
  • lines 34–44: generating the token. Its content is a dictionary of claims about the user. Some have standardized names: [sub] (*subject*), the user’s identifier; [iat] (*issued at*), the creation date; [exp] (*expiration*), the expiration date. The others are arbitrary: in this case, the name and role. [jwt.encode] generates the token and signs it using the algorithm [HS256] (HMAC-SHA256, a signature using a shared secret key). Dates must be time-zone-aware dates: [datetime.now(timezone.utc)];
  • Lines 48–30: Token verification. [jwt.decode] verifies the signature and expiration date, then returns the assertions. Any anomaly (forged, expired, or malformed token) raises an exception from the [InvalidTokenError] family. The [algorithms] parameter specifies the accepted algorithms: without it, an attacker could create a token that declares a different algorithm (or even none at all, [none]).

docs.title: 8.1.4. Security: auth/securite.py
docs.text:
# auth/securite.py: the user for each request, and protection of actions
from functools import wraps

from flask import g, redirect, request, url_for

from auth.service import COOKIE, auth_service


def enregistrer(app):

     # before each action: the cookie token -> g.utilisateur (its claims), or None
    @app.before_request
    def lire_jeton():
        jeton = request.cookies.get(COOKIE)
        g.utilisateur = auth_service().verifier(jeton) if jeton else None


# a decorator: the action is executed only for an authenticated user;
# otherwise, redirect to the login page
def connexion_requise(action):
    @wraps(action)
    def action_protegee(*args, **kwargs):
        if g.utilisateur is None:
            reponse = redirect(url_for("auth.formulaire"))
             # a cookie is present but invalid (expired or forged token): it is deleted
            if COOKIE in request.cookies:
                reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE)
            return reponse
        return action(*args, **kwargs)

    return action_protegee
  • lines 13–15: Before each action, the cookie token is verified; [g.utilisateur] contains the claims of a valid token, or [None]. This function does not reject anything: it establishes who the user is. This is authentication;
  • lines 20–31: the decorator that requires an authenticated user. For an anonymous visitor, it does not return the action but instead redirects to the login page. If the browser sent a cookie, it means the token is invalid (expired or forged): we take this opportunity to delete it ([delete_cookie] sends an empty cookie that has already expired).

docs.title: 8.1.5. The controllers
docs.text:
# controllers/auth.py: login and logout
from flask import Blueprint, redirect, render_template, request, url_for

from auth.service import COOKIE, auth_service

auth = Blueprint("auth", __name__)


@auth.get("/")
def accueil():
    return redirect(url_for("profil.afficher"))


@auth.get("/login")
def formulaire():
    return render_template("auth/login.html")


@auth.post("/login")
def connexion():
    login = request.form.get("login")
    utilisateur = auth_service().valider(login, request.form.get("motDePasse"))
    if utilisateur is None:
         # A deliberately vague message: it doesn’t specify whether it’s the username or the password
        return render_template("auth/login.html", login=login,
                               erreur="Login ou mot de passe incorrect.")
    reponse = redirect(url_for("profil.afficher"))
     # the token, stored in a cookie: the page’s JavaScript cannot read it
     # (httponly); it is not included in requests like POST coming from other sites
     # (samesite); it disappears when the token expires (max_age)
    reponse.set_cookie(COOKIE, auth_service().creer_jeton(utilisateur), httponly=True,
                       samesite="Lax", max_age=auth_service().duree)
    return reponse


# Logout: POST only (a simple link placed on another site
# log the user out without their knowledge); the cookie is deleted
@auth.post("/logout")
def deconnexion():
    reponse = redirect(url_for("auth.formulaire"))
    reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE)
    return reponse
  • lines 20–26: the login. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with the entered username and a deliberately vague message: saying “unknown username” would reveal to a hacker which usernames exist;
  • lines 27–32: if successful, the token is stored in a cookie, with a redirect to the protected page (schema PRG). The cookie is [httponly]: the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token against script injection (XSS); it is [samesite="Lax"]: the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site, which protects the application against CSRF attacks (example 18); its lifetime ([max_age], which accepts a [timedelta]) is that of the token. In production, for HTTPS, we would add [secure=True]: the cookie would never be sent over an unencrypted connection;
  • lines 38–41: Logging out deletes the cookie. This is a POST action: a simple link to [/logout], placed on another site or within an image, cannot log the user out without their knowledge. Note a limitation of tokens: the token itself remains valid until it expires. Someone who has made a copy of it could still use it. That is why their lifetime is limited.
# controllers/profil.py: a page reserved for authenticated users
from flask import Blueprint, g, render_template

from auth.securite import connexion_requise

profil = Blueprint("profil", __name__)


@profil.get("/profil")
@connexion_requise
def afficher():
     # g.utilisateur: the token’s claims, already verified (see auth/securite.py)
    return render_template("profil/profil.html", nom=g.utilisateur["nom"],
                           admin=g.utilisateur["role"] == "ADMIN", claims=g.utilisateur)
  • line 10: the page is protected;
  • line 13: the action uses [g.utilisateur], ensuring it is not [None].

docs.title: 8.1.7. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s request the protected page [/profil] without being logged in:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 199
Location: /login
...

An incorrect password:

Login successful. With [curl], we save the received cookie to a file:

curl -i -c jeton.txt -d "login=marie&motDePasse=marie" http://localhost:5000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 201
Location: /profil
Set-Cookie: jeton=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJtYXJpZSIsIm5vbSI6Ik1hcmllIFBcdTAwZTlsaXNzaWVyIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIiLCJpYXQiOjE3OTA0MzAwMTgsImV4cCI6MTc5MDQzMzYxOH0.Rw_mzqGIMz1o1T6VgyhyT0G_r42ZwhdriV9zri08uos; Expires=Sat, 26 Sep 2026 14:40:18 GMT; Max-Age=3600; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...

The token consists of three parts, separated by periods, each encoded in Base64: the header, the content, and the signature. The first two parts can be decoded without any key:

{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
{"sub":"marie","nom":"Marie Pélissier","role":"USER","iat":1790430018,"exp":1790433618}

Dates are expressed in seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970; the expiration time is one hour after creation. In the browser, the profile page displays this same content:

A malicious user modifies their token: they replace the role ***[USER]*** in the content with ***[ADMIN]***, re-encode this part in Base64, and keep the original signature. The server recalculates the signature of the modified content, which no longer matches:

curl -i -b "jeton=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.<contenu modifié>.Rw_mzqGIMz1o1T6VgyhyT0G_r42ZwhdriV9zri08uos" http://localhost:5000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 199
Location: /login
Set-Cookie: jeton=; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/
...

The forged token is rejected and deleted. To generate a valid signature, one would need to know the secret key—hence the importance of keeping it secret and choosing a long, random key.

docs.title: 8.2. Example 26: Roles
docs.text: Example 26 adds an administration page, restricted to the role ADMIN. Only new or modified files are displayed.

docs.title: 8.2.1. A decorator with a parameter: auth/securite.py
docs.text:
# auth/securite.py: the user for each request, and action protection
from functools import wraps

from flask import abort, g, redirect, request, url_for

from auth.service import COOKIE, auth_service


def enregistrer(app):

     # before each action: the cookie token -> g.utilisateur (its claims), or None
    @app.before_request
    def lire_jeton():
        jeton = request.cookies.get(COOKIE)
        g.utilisateur = auth_service().verifier(jeton) if jeton else None


# a decorator: the action is executed only for an authenticated user;
# otherwise, redirect to the login page
def connexion_requise(action):
    @wraps(action)
    def action_protegee(*args, **kwargs):
        if g.utilisateur is None:
            reponse = redirect(url_for("auth.formulaire"))
             # a cookie is present but invalid (expired or forged token): it is deleted
            if COOKIE in request.cookies:
                reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE)
            return reponse
        return action(*args, **kwargs)

    return action_protegee


# a decorator at PARAMÈTRE: @role_requis("ADMIN"). role_requis("ADMIN") returns
# the decorator itself, which receives the action. It is used as APRÈS (sub)
# @connexion_requise: the user is then necessarily authenticated
def role_requis(role: str):
    def decorateur(action):
        @wraps(action)
        def action_protegee(*args, **kwargs):
            if g.utilisateur["role"] != role:
                abort(403)  # access denied
            return action(*args, **kwargs)

        return action_protegee

    return decorateur
  • Lines 37–47: [@role_requis("ADMIN")] has one parameter. The expression following [@] is evaluated first: [role_requis("ADMIN")] returns a function, [decorateur], which is the decorator itself, applied to the action. We therefore have three nested functions: [role_requis] receives the role, [decorateur] receives the action, and [action_protegee] receives the request parameters and performs the work. Each has access to the variables of the functions that contain it ([role], [action]);
  • Line 42: An authenticated user who does not have the requested role receives a 403 error (*Forbidden*). This is significantly different from an anonymous user, who is redirected to the login page: logging in would serve no purpose, since the user is already authenticated.

docs.title: 8.2.2. The controller: controllers/admin.py
docs.text:
# controllers/admin.py: a page reserved for the ADMIN role
from flask import Blueprint, g, render_template

from auth.securite import connexion_requise, role_requis

admin = Blueprint("admin", __name__)


# Decorators are applied from bottom to top: role_requis wraps the action,
# then connexion_requise wraps the whole thing. At runtime, it is therefore
# connexion_requise that verifies EN PREMIER that the user is authenticated
@admin.get("/admin")
@connexion_requise
@role_requis("ADMIN")
def afficher():
    return render_template("admin/admin.html", nom=g.utilisateur["nom"])
  • Lines 12–14: Decorators are applied from bottom to top: [role_requis] wraps the action, then [connexion_requise] wraps the entire structure. At runtime, the order is reversed: the outer wrapper, [connexion_requise], executes first. So when [role_requis] runs, the user is necessarily authenticated, and [g.utilisateur] is not [None].

docs.title: 8.2.3. The error page: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 26
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, render_template

from auth import securite
from auth.service import AuthService
from auth.utilisateurs import UtilisateursService
from controllers.admin import admin
from controllers.auth import auth
from controllers.profil import profil

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
     # the configuration: the file config.py, followed by the environment variables
     # that begin with FLASK_ (FLASK_JWT_SECRET replaces JWT_SECRET)
    app.config.from_pyfile("config.py")
    app.config.from_prefixed_env()
     # authentication services
    utilisateurs = UtilisateursService()
    app.extensions["auth"] = AuthService(utilisateurs, app.config["JWT_SECRET"],
                                         app.config["JWT_DUREE_MINUTES"])
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(auth)
    app.register_blueprint(profil)
    app.register_blueprint(admin)
     # the user for each request, read from the cookie token
    securite.enregistrer(app)

     # insufficient role: abort(403) (see auth/securite.py) -> our error page
    @app.errorhandler(403)
    def acces_refuse(e):
        return render_template("erreur.html", code=403), 403

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 37–39: A registered error handler for a specific code—error 403—displays our page.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and Attempt Limits
docs.text:
A login form is a target: a program can try thousands of passwords per minute (brute-force attack). Two protections complement each other:

  • a CAPTCHA (*Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart*): an image containing a distorted code that is easy for a human to read but difficult for a program;
  • an attempt limit: after three failed attempts, the client’s address IP is blocked for one minute.

Example 27 is based on Example 25 (without the administration page) and adds these two security measures.
