docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# repositories/creneau_repository.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Layer DAO of entity [Creneau].
# =========================================================================
from sqlalchemy import delete, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, joinedload

from rdvmedecins.entities import Creneau


class CreneauRepository:

     # an appointment slot and its doctor
    def lire(self, session: Session, id: int) -> Creneau | None:
        return session.get(Creneau, id, options=[joinedload(Creneau.medecin)])

     # a doctor’s time slots, in chronological order
    def lister_par_medecin(self, session: Session, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]:
        requete = (select(Creneau).where(Creneau.id_medecin == id_medecin)
                   .order_by(Creneau.hdebut, Creneau.mdebut))
        return list(session.scalars(requete))

     # deletes all of a doctor’s time slots (deleting a doctor):
        # DELETE FROM slots WHERE id_medecin = ?
    def supprimer_par_medecin(self, session: Session, id_medecin: int):
        session.execute(delete(Creneau).where(Creneau.id_medecin == id_medecin))

An appointment slot (with a doctor), a doctor’s appointment slots in chronological order, and the deletion of a doctor’s appointment slots (when the doctor is removed).

docs.title: 11.11.5. repositories/rv_repository.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# repositories/rv_repository.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Layer DAO of the entity [Rv] (an appointment).
#
# join(Rv.creneau): a join on SQL, derived from RELATION between
# the two classes (SQLAlchemy knows the foreign key). contains_eager:
# the columns of the joined table are used to populate the relation
# (rv.creneau), without a new query.
# =========================================================================
from datetime import date

from sqlalchemy import delete, func, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, contains_eager, joinedload

from rdvmedecins.entities import Creneau, Rv


class RvRepository:

     # an appointment, its client, and its time slot
    def lire(self, session: Session, id: int) -> Rv | None:
        return session.get(Rv, id, options=[joinedload(Rv.client), joinedload(Rv.creneau)])

     # a doctor’s appointments on a given day, including the client and time slot.
     # The [rv] table does not directly reference the doctor: it goes through the time slot.
    def rv_medecin_jour(self, session: Session, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]:
        requete = (select(Rv).join(Rv.creneau)
                   .options(contains_eager(Rv.creneau), joinedload(Rv.client))
                   .where(Creneau.id_medecin == id_medecin, Rv.jour == jour))
        return list(session.scalars(requete))

     # a client’s appointments starting on or after the day [depuis], in
     # chronological order, with the time slot ET and the doctor assigned to that time slot
    def rv_a_venir_client(self, session: Session, id_client: int, depuis: date) -> list[Rv]:
        requete = (select(Rv).join(Rv.creneau)
                   .options(contains_eager(Rv.creneau).joinedload(Creneau.medecin))
                   .where(Rv.id_client == id_client, Rv.jour >= depuis)
                   .order_by(Rv.jour, Creneau.hdebut, Creneau.mdebut))
        return list(session.scalars(requete))

     # number of a client's appointments starting on or including the day [depuis]
    def compter_a_venir_client(self, session: Session, id_client: int, depuis: date) -> int:
        requete = select(func.count(Rv.id)).where(Rv.id_client == id_client, Rv.jour >= depuis)
        return session.scalar(requete)

     # number of appointments (past or future) for a doctor
    def compter_par_medecin(self, session: Session, id_medecin: int) -> int:
        requete = select(func.count(Rv.id)).join(Rv.creneau).where(Creneau.id_medecin == id_medecin)
        return session.scalar(requete)

    def ajouter(self, session: Session, rv: Rv) -> Rv:
        session.add(rv)
        return rv

     # deletes an appointment: DELETE FROM rv WHERE id = ?
    def supprimer(self, session: Session, id: int):
        session.execute(delete(Rv).where(Rv.id == id))

     # deletes TOUS a client’s appointments (past and future)
    def supprimer_par_client(self, session: Session, id_client: int):
        session.execute(delete(Rv).where(Rv.id_client == id_client))
  • Lines 27–31: a doctor’s appointments on a given day. The table [rv] does not directly reference the doctor: it goes through the appointment slot. [join(Rv.creneau)] writes the join based on the relationship; the filter applies to a column in the joined table ([Creneau.id_medecin]). [contains_eager] reuses the join to populate [rv.creneau]; [joinedload] loads the client: the schedule is built in a single query, SQL;
  • lines 35–39: a client’s upcoming appointments, with their time slots and the physician assigned to each slot;
  • lines 43–45: [func.count] generates the functions SQL, [COUNT], and [session.scalar] (in the singular); [session.scalar] returns the first column of the first row: the count;
  • lines 48–50: the number of appointments for a doctor, to determine whether the doctor can be deleted;
  • lines 61–62: the deletion of a client’s appointments (when the client is deleted).

docs.title: 11.11.6. repositories/user_repository.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# repositories/user_repository.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# DAO layer of the [User] entity. Create (or delete) a doctor or a
# client also creates (or deletes) their account—see business/service.py.
# =========================================================================
from sqlalchemy import delete, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from rdvmedecins.entities import User


class UserRepository:

     # None if no user has this login
    def lire_par_login(self, session: Session, login: str) -> User | None:
        return session.scalars(select(User).where(User.login == login)).first()

    def ajouter(self, session: Session, user: User) -> User:
        session.add(user)
        return user

    def supprimer(self, session: Session, id: int):
        session.execute(delete(User).where(User.id == id))

Reading a user by their login (for login), adding and deleting an account.

docs.title: 11.12. The business layer
docs.text: The [metier] folder contains the business rules, and only those rules. It does not recognize [Flask], HTML, or the HTTP query: it could be used as-is in a command-line application or in a API.

docs.title: 11.12.1. metier/dates.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/dates.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Today’s date. It is used for RÈGLES, DE, and GESTION (no appointment
# in the past; only one appointment per patient at VENIR): it therefore resides
# in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.
# =========================================================================
from datetime import date


# today’s date, in the server’s time zone
def aujourdhui() -> date:
    return date.today()

The current date is used for two business rules (no appointments in the past, only one upcoming appointment per patient): it belongs in the business layer. Isolating it in a function has another advantage: an automated test could replace it with a fixed date.

docs.title: 11.12.2. business/exception.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/exception.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The exception thrown by the business layer when a RÈGLE DE GESTION is
# violated (username already taken, doctor still has appointments, time slot
# already reserved...). It does not carry text, but a CLÉ of
# translation (e.g., "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN"): it is the web layer that
# will translate into French or English when the page is displayed
# (see i18n/fr.json, i18n/en.json).
#
# A MetierException is not an error: it is a normal response
# ("this login is already taken"), displayed to the user. Any other
# exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.
# =========================================================================


class MetierException(Exception):

    def __init__(self, cle: str, parametres: dict[str, str] | None = None):
        super().__init__(cle)
         # message translation key
        self.cle = cle
         # any message parameters ({minutes}...)
        self.parametres = parametres or {}

The business layer exception does not carry text, as in Example 28, but rather a translation key ([ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN]) and any parameters: the business layer does not know in which language the user is viewing the page. The web layer will translate the key. [super().__init__(cle)] passes the key to the constructor of the [Exception] class: this is the value that is displayed if the exception is logged.

A [MetierException] is not an error: it is a normal response (“this username is already taken”), which is displayed to the user. Any other exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.

# business domain/donnees.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The data entered in the "doctor" or "client" form, such as
# the web layer transmits it to the business layer.
# =========================================================================
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DonneesPersonne:
    titre: str  # Mr., Mrs., Ms.
    nom: str
    prenom: str
     # creation: optional (None), defaults to the name in lowercase
     # modification: optional; the login remains unchanged if omitted
    login: str | None = None
     # creation: optional; defaults to the login
     # update: optional; the password remains unchanged if omitted
    password: str | None = None
     # modification: the version of the record at the time the form was
     # was displayed (optimistic lock, see entities/base.py)

docs.title: 11.12.4. business/metier.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business layer/metier.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The CONTRAT of the business layer: readings, calendar, appointments, management
# for doctors and clients.
#
# A protocol describes the methods an object must have, without specifying how
# they are implemented (the equivalent of an interface). MetierService (the
# business layer) and ApplicationModel (the web layer cache)
# are both compliant. Python does not check anything at runtime: these are
# the analysis tools (such as the one from VS Code, for example) that flag a discrepancy.
#
# T | None: a result that may be absent (a doctor who doesn’t exist...).
# =========================================================================
from datetime import date
from typing import Protocol

from rdvmedecins.domain.agenda import AgendaMedecinJour
from rdvmedecins.entities import Client, Creneau, Medecin, Rv
from rdvmedecins.metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne


class Metier(Protocol):

     # ------------------------------------------------ readings
    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]: ...

    def get_all_medecins(self) -> list[Medecin]: ...

    def get_all_creneaux(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]: ...

    def get_rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]: ...

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    def get_medecin_by_id(self, id: int) -> Medecin | None: ...

    def get_rv_by_id(self, id: int) -> Rv | None: ...

    def get_creneau_by_id(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None: ...

    def get_agenda_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> AgendaMedecinJour | None: ...

     # the client (patient) whose user account is [id_user]
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Client | None: ...

     # a client’s appointments, for today or in the future, with time slot and doctor
    def get_rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int) -> list[Rv]: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
     # generates a MetierException if:
       # - the day has passed ("ERRORS.PAST_DATE");
       # - the patient already has an upcoming appointment ("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT");
       # - the time slot is already booked for that day ("ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED").
    def ajouter_rv(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv: ...

    def supprimer_rv(self, rv: Rv) -> None: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
     # creates a user account for the doctor ET (role DOCTOR)
    def ajouter_medecin(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin: ...

     # modifies the doctor ET's user account
    def modifier_medecin(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin: ...

     # deletes the doctor, his time slots, and his account (ET) — rejected if he has appointments
    def supprimer_medecin(self, id: int) -> None: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ clients
     # (ADMIN; ajouter_client is also used to register a patient,
     # modifier_client and supprimer_client to the patient on his or her own behalf)
     # creates the client ET and their user account (role USER)
    def ajouter_client(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client: ...

    def modifier_client(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client: ...

     # deletes the client, their account ET, and all their appointments (past and future)
    def supprimer_client(self, id: int) -> None: ...
  • Line 23: The business layer contract: a list of its methods, along with their parameters and return values. A [Protocol] (standard module [typing]) is the [Python] equivalent of an interface: it describes the methods an object must have, without specifying how they are implemented. A class conforms to it as long as it has these methods, without having to declare it (this is known as structural typing, or *duck typing*: “if it walks like a duck…”). Two classes conform to it: [MetierService], the business layer, and [ApplicationModel], the web layer cache (discussed later). [Python] does not check anything at runtime: it is the analysis tools, such as the one in [Visual Studio Code], that flag a discrepancy;
  • line 26: the body of a protocol method is reduced to [...] (the [Ellipsis] object of [Python], which does nothing);
  • lines 55–78: the comments document the business logic and error codes for each method.

docs.title: 11.12.5. business/service.py
docs.text:
The business layer implementation. This is the most important file in the application.

# =========================================================================
# business logic/service.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Implementation of the business layer.
#
# The management of doctors and clients follows three management rules:
#
#    1. A person (doctor or client) and their user account are
#       TOUJOURS together: they are created, modified, and deleted together, in
#       a single TRANSACTION—either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
#    2. The login is unique throughout the application, and two doctors (or
#       two clients) cannot have the same first and last names;
#    3. Deletion:
#       - A MÉDECIN with appointments cannot be deleted (their
#         patients would lose their appointments without being notified): you must
#         cancel them first. Its time slots disappear along with it;
#       - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears along with TOUS its appointments (past and
#         future) — regardless of whether the deletion is initiated by the ADMIN or the patient
#         .
#
# And two rules for scheduling appointments, regardless of the role of
# the person making the reservation (ADMIN, DOCTOR, or the patient themselves):
#    4. No appointments in the past;
#    5. A patient can have only one upcoming appointment at a time.
#
# Doctors and patients follow exactly the same rules: the common code
# is written UNE times (private methods _xxx_personne), and configured by a
# small “descriptor” that indicates what type of person we are dealing with.
#
# The TRANSACTIONS files are opened using the _transaction method (at the end of the
# file), which also translates into MetierException the errors that the database
# reports when SQL commands are sent to it.
# =========================================================================
import re
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import StaleDataError

from rdvmedecins.auth.mots_de_passe import hacher
from rdvmedecins.domain.agenda import AgendaMedecinJour, CreneauMedecinJour
from rdvmedecins.entities import Client, Creneau, Medecin, Personne, Role, Rv, User
from rdvmedecins.metier import dates
from rdvmedecins.metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne
from rdvmedecins.metier.exception import MetierException
from rdvmedecins.repositories.client_repository import ClientRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.creneau_repository import CreneauRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.medecin_repository import MedecinRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.personne_repository import PersonneRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.rv_repository import RvRepository
from rdvmedecins.repositories.user_repository import UserRepository


# everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for management rules
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Descripteur:
    dao: PersonneRepository
    fabrique: type[Personne]  # Doctor or Client
    role: Role  # DOCTOR or USER
    cle_introuvable: str  # message if the person does not exist
    cle_existe_deja: str  # message if the same first and last names already exist
     # optional (None): if present, the deletion is REFUSÉE as long as the
     # person has appointments (compter_rv > 0), with the message cle_avec_rv
    compter_rv: Callable[[Session, int], int] | None
    cle_avec_rv: str | None
     # optional: what to delete from the person (the rows that
     # refer to them via a foreign key)
    avant_suppression: Callable[[Session, int], None] | None


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Database errors -> MetierException
#
# When a constraint UNIQUE rejects a write operation, SQLAlchemy raises a
# IntegrityError, whose attribute [orig] is the original error, that of the
# driver PyMySQL. Its message cites the NOM of the constraint:
#    Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'medecins.unq_medecins_prenom_nom'
# (MySQL prefixes the name with the table name, MariaDB does not). This is why
# this reason that the script SQL NOMME has all these constraints.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
MESSAGES_CONTRAINTES = {
    "unq_users_login": "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN",
    "unq_medecins_prenom_nom": "ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
    "unq_clients_prenom_nom": "ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
    "unq1_rv": "ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED",
}

CONTRAINTE = re.compile(r"for key '(?:[^'.]*\.)?([^']+)'")


class MetierService:

     # all dependencies are provided by the application factory
     # (see rdvmedecins/__init__.py): this is “main-style”
     # manual" style. sessions: the session factory from SQLAlchemy.
    def __init__(self, sessions: sessionmaker, medecins: MedecinRepository,
                 clients: ClientRepository, creneaux: CreneauRepository, rvs: RvRepository,
                 users: UserRepository):
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._medecins = medecins
        self._clients = clients
        self._creneaux = creneaux
        self._rvs = rvs
        self._users = users

        self._medecin = Descripteur(
            dao=medecins, fabrique=Medecin, role=Role.DOCTOR,
            cle_introuvable="ERRORS.DOCTOR_NOT_FOUND",
            cle_existe_deja="ERRORS.DOCTOR_ALREADY_EXISTS",
            compter_rv=rvs.compter_par_medecin,
            cle_avec_rv="ERRORS.DOCTOR_HAS_APPOINTMENTS",
             # A walk-in doctor may still have time slots:
             # they no longer make sense without it, so we remove them along with it (otherwise
             # the foreign key creneaux.id_medecin would prevent the deletion)
            avant_suppression=creneaux.supprimer_par_medecin)

        self._client = Descripteur(
            dao=clients, fabrique=Client, role=Role.USER,
            cle_introuvable="ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND",
            cle_existe_deja="ERRORS.PATIENT_ALREADY_EXISTS",
             # no compter_rv: deleting a client is never denied;
             # their appointments (past and future) are deleted along with them (otherwise
             # the foreign key rv.id_client would prevent deletion)
            compter_rv=None, cle_avec_rv=None,
            avant_suppression=rvs.supprimer_par_client)

    # =======================================================================
     # read operations: a session, lasting the time of the read; the read objects remain
     # available afterward (expire_on_commit=False, see rdvmedecins/__init__.py)
    # =======================================================================

    def _lecture[R](self, travail: Callable[[Session], R]) -> R:
        with self._sessions() as session:
            return travail(session)

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return self._lecture(self._clients.lister)

    def get_all_medecins(self) -> list[Medecin]:
        return self._lecture(self._medecins.lister)

    def get_all_creneaux(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._creneaux.lister_par_medecin(s, id_medecin))

    def get_rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._rvs.rv_medecin_jour(s, id_medecin, jour))

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._clients.lire(s, id))

    def get_medecin_by_id(self, id: int) -> Medecin | None:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._medecins.lire(s, id))

    def get_rv_by_id(self, id: int) -> Rv | None:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._rvs.lire(s, id))

    def get_creneau_by_id(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._creneaux.lire(s, id))

    def get_client_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Client | None:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._clients.lire_par_user(s, id_user))

    def get_rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int) -> list[Rv]:
        return self._lecture(lambda s: self._rvs.rv_a_venir_client(s, id_client, dates.aujourdhui()))

     # a doctor’s schedule for a given day: their time slots, and for each one the
     # appointment scheduled for that day (None if the doctor is available)
    def get_agenda_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> AgendaMedecinJour | None:
        medecin = self.get_medecin_by_id(id_medecin)
        if medecin is None:
            return None
        creneaux_horaires = self.get_all_creneaux(id_medecin)
         # slot number -> appointment scheduled for that slot (a "read-only" dictionary)
        reservations = {rv.id_creneau: rv for rv in self.get_rv_medecin_jour(id_medecin, jour)}
        creneaux_medecin_jour = [CreneauMedecinJour(creneau, reservations.get(creneau.id))
                                 for creneau in creneaux_horaires]
        return AgendaMedecinJour(medecin, jour, creneaux_medecin_jour)

    # =======================================================================
     # appointment
    # =======================================================================

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # appointment scheduling, in a transaction:
        # 1. no past appointments;
        # 2. on the patient’s line (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the
           # same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs,
           # double-clicking...), the second transaction waits for the
           # first one—and then sees the appointment it just created;
        # 3. only one upcoming appointment per patient;
        # 4. Finally, the insertion. If the time slot has just been taken by a AUTRE
           # patient, it is the constraint SQL unq1_rv (day, id_creneau) that
           # prevents insertion—translated to MetierException by _transaction.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def ajouter_rv(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv:
        def travail(session: Session) -> Rv:
            aujourdhui = dates.aujourdhui()
            if jour < aujourdhui:
                raise MetierException("ERRORS.PAST_DATE")
            id_patient = self._clients.verrouiller(session, client.id)
            if id_patient is None:
                raise MetierException("ERRORS.PATIENT_NOT_FOUND")
            if self._rvs.compter_a_venir_client(session, id_patient, aujourdhui) > 0:
                raise MetierException("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT")
             # all you need is the slot ID and the patient ID to write
             # foreign keys: no need to re-read these objects in the session
            return self._rvs.ajouter(session, Rv(jour=jour, id_creneau=creneau.id,
                                                 id_client=id_patient))

        return self._transaction(travail)

    def supprimer_rv(self, rv: Rv) -> None:
        self._transaction(lambda session: self._rvs.supprimer(session, rv.id))

    # =======================================================================
     # doctors and clients—public methods delegate to
     # shared private methods, with the correct descriptor
    # =======================================================================

    def ajouter_medecin(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        return self._ajouter_personne(self._medecin, donnees)

    def modifier_medecin(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        return self._modifier_personne(self._medecin, id, donnees)

    def supprimer_medecin(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._supprimer_personne(self._medecin, id)

    def ajouter_client(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        return self._ajouter_personne(self._client, donnees)

    def modifier_client(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        return self._modifier_personne(self._client, id, donnees)

     # the client, their account ET all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient
     # themselves via “Manage My Account”: same method, same rule)
    def supprimer_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._supprimer_personne(self._client, id)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # creation: the user account ET for the person, in the UNE transaction.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _ajouter_personne(self, d: Descripteur, donnees: DonneesPersonne):
        nom = donnees.nom.strip().upper()
        prenom = donnees.prenom.strip()
         # the rules for the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = name in lowercase,
         # password = login—unless the user has entered others
        login = (donnees.login or nom).lower()
        password = donnees.password or login

        def travail(session: Session):
            self._verifier_personne_unique(session, d, prenom, nom, None)
            self._verifier_login_libre(session, login)
            user = User(login=login, password=hacher(password), nom=f"{prenom} {nom}", role=d.role)
            personne = d.fabrique(titre=donnees.titre, nom=nom, prenom=prenom, user=user)
             # the person references their account: SQLAlchemy first enters the
             # account (to find out their ID), then the person
            d.dao.ajouter(session, personne)
             # flush: the INSERT messages are sent immediately (and not to COMMIT); a
             # constraint violation therefore clears its error ICI
            session.flush()
            return personne

        return self._transaction(travail)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # update: the user ET updates their account (the displayed name "first name NOM"
     # must follow; the username and password only change if they were
     # entered).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _modifier_personne(self, d: Descripteur, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne):
        def travail(session: Session):
            personne = d.dao.lire(session, id)
            if personne is None:
                raise MetierException(d.cle_introuvable)

             # optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer the same as the
             # form, someone has modified this record in the meantime—the system rejects
             # rather than silently overwriting their changes.
             # (If the concurrent modification occurs APRÈS during this read, it is
             # the "WHERE version = ..." clause in the UPDATE that detects it.)
            if donnees.version is not None and donnees.version != personne.version:
                raise MetierException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE")

            nom = donnees.nom.strip().upper()
            prenom = donnees.prenom.strip()
            self._verifier_personne_unique(session, d, prenom, nom, id)

             # we simply modify the objects: they are “tracked” by the
             # session, which will itself send the necessary UPDATE
            personne.titre = donnees.titre
            personne.nom = nom
            personne.prenom = prenom

            user = personne.user
            user.nom = f"{prenom} {nom}"
            if donnees.login and donnees.login.lower() != user.login:
                login = donnees.login.lower()
                self._verifier_login_libre(session, login)
                user.login = login
            if donnees.password:
                user.password = hacher(donnees.password)
            session.flush()
            return personne

        return self._transaction(travail)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # deletion, in the UNE transaction, in the order dictated by the
     # foreign keys:
        # 1. possible rejection if there are still available appointments (doctor);
        # 2. information identifying the person (a doctor’s time slots,
           # for a client);
        # 3. the person (who references their account);
        # 4. their account.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _supprimer_personne(self, d: Descripteur, id: int) -> None:
        def travail(session: Session):
            personne = d.dao.lire(session, id)
            if personne is None:
                raise MetierException(d.cle_introuvable)
            if d.compter_rv is not None and d.compter_rv(session, id) > 0:
                raise MetierException(d.cle_avec_rv)
            if d.avant_suppression is not None:
                d.avant_suppression(session, id)
            d.dao.supprimer(session, id)
            self._users.supprimer(session, personne.id_user)

        self._transaction(travail)

     # Rejects first and last names already used by a AUTRE person of the same type
     # (id_courant: the person being edited, who obviously has the
     # right to keep their own first and last names; None for a new creation)
    @staticmethod
    def _verifier_personne_unique(session: Session, d: Descripteur, prenom: str, nom: str,
                                  id_courant: int | None):
        homonyme = d.dao.homonyme(session, prenom, nom)
        if homonyme is not None and homonyme.id != id_courant:
            raise MetierException(d.cle_existe_deja)

    def _verifier_login_libre(self, session: Session, login: str):
        if self._users.lire_par_login(session, login) is not None:
            raise MetierException("ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN")

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # executes [travail] in a transaction:
        # sessions.begin() -> a session and its transaction (START TRANSACTION);
        # upon exiting the `with` block: COMMIT if everything went well; if an
        # an exception is thrown (including MetierException), ROLLBACK: nothing is written.
    #
     # The "free login" and "unique first name + last name" checks are performed AVANT
     # the entry, to provide a clear message. But two ADMIN entries could
     # register the same login (or the same doctor) at the same time: in this
     # rare case, a uniqueness constraint SQL rejects the second
     # write. We therefore intercept errors from the database AUTOUR of the
     # transaction, to translate them into the same MetierException:
        # - StaleDataError: the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." has
          # modified any rows (optimistic lock);
        # - IntegrityError: a database constraint rejected the write.
     # Any other error is a true anomaly: it is allowed to be reported.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _transaction[R](self, travail: Callable[[Session], R]) -> R:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                return travail(session)
        except StaleDataError:
            raise MetierException("ERRORS.CONCURRENT_UPDATE")
        except IntegrityError as e:
            correspondance = CONTRAINTE.search(str(e.orig))
            if correspondance and correspondance.group(1) in MESSAGES_CONTRAINTES:
                raise MetierException(MESSAGES_CONTRAINTES[correspondance.group(1)])
            raise

docs.title: 11.12.5.1. The descriptors
docs.text:
Doctors and clients follow exactly the same business rules, with a few minor differences: a different DAO, a different role for their account, different error messages, and a different deletion rule. Rather than writing each method twice, the common code is written once (the methods [_ajouter_personne], [_modifier_personne], [_supprimer_personne]) and configured by a descriptor that specifies which type of person is being handled:

  • lines 59–71: the descriptor is an immutable [dataclass]. Three of its fields are functions: [Callable[[Session, int], int]] is the type of a function that takes a session and an integer, and returns an integer. [compter_rv] counts a person’s appointments (to prevent the deletion of a doctor who has any); [avant_suppression] deletes references to the person (a doctor’s time slots, a client’s appointments);
  • lines 109–118: the doctors’ descriptor. [rvs.compter_par_medecin] is a method associated with the object [rvs] (Example 22): a function that will receive the session and the ID;
  • lines 120–128: the one for clients: no deletion denial ([compter_rv=None]), but the prior deletion of all their appointments.

docs.title: 11.12.5.2. Read operations and the calendar
docs.text:
• lines 135–137: the reads are handled by a small generic method: [R] is the result type, which is the same as that of the function [travail]. The session is opened by [self._sessions()] (without [begin]) while the function is executing, then closed by the block [with]. [SQLAlchemy] still starts a transaction on the first request ([BEGIN (implicit)] in the console); since nothing was written, closing the session cancels it ([ROLLBACK]): these are the lines the console displays when the application starts;
  • lines 139–167: each read instructs [_lecture] to call the method DAO. When the DAO method has parameters other than the session, an anonymous function ([lambda s: ...]) provides them;
  • Lines 171–180: A doctor’s schedule for a single day. The day’s appointments are stored in a dictionary ([{clé: valeur for ...}]) that associates each time slot number with its corresponding appointment; Each time slot is then associated with its appointment, or with [None] ([reservations.get(creneau.id)]). Three reads, across three sessions: any inconsistency between them (an appointment scheduled between two reads) would be inconsequential, since the schedule is merely a display.

docs.title: 11.12.5.3. Scheduling an appointment
docs.text:
• Lines 198–213: The method defines an internal function, [travail], which contains the operations to be performed in the transaction, and passes it to the method [_transaction] (see below). The rules, in order: - No appointments in the past ([jour < aujourdhui]: the dates in [Python] are compared using the usual operators); - the patient’s record is locked ([verrouiller], see [ClientRepository]): if the same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, a double-click), the second transaction waits for the first one to complete and then sees the appointment it created; - only one upcoming appointment per patient; - finally, the insertion. The appointment is created using the slot ID and the patient ID: it is sufficient to know the values of the foreign keys; there is no need to re-read the objects. The named parameters of the constructor ([Rv(jour=..., id_creneau=...)]) are provided by [SQLAlchemy] to any entity that does not have its own constructor.
  • There is one remaining scenario: the time slot has just been taken by another patient between the time the calendar is displayed and the time the reservation is made. In this case, the database constraint [unq1_rv] prevents the insertion during the [COMMIT] operation. The [_transaction] method translates this error into [MetierException];
  • lines 215–216: canceling an appointment. Permission checks (a patient can only cancel their own appointments) are performed by the web layer, which knows the user.

docs.title: 11.12.5.4. Management of doctors and clients
docs.text:
• lines 223–241: public methods delegate to common methods, using the correct descriptor;
  • lines 246–267: creation. The last name is capitalized, and spaces are removed from the first name; the default username is the last name in lowercase, and the password is the username (the rule for demo accounts in the SQL script). In the transaction: validations (no homonyms, free login), followed by the creation of the account and the person. The person receives their account through their relationship ([user=user]): [SQLAlchemy] knows it must first insert the account to obtain its ID, then the person. [session.flush()] sends [INSERT] immediately: a violated constraint triggers an error in the transaction, and the returned person has its ID;
  • Lines 274–309: the update. The form version is compared to the database version (optimistic lock, example 28); then we simply update the retrieved objects: they are tracked by the session, which will itself send the necessary [UPDATE] records. The displayed account name follows the first name and last name; the login and password change only if they have been entered;
  • lines 320–332: deletion, in the order dictated by the foreign keys: possible rejection (a doctor who has appointments), deletion of the references to the person, the person themselves, and then their account. In the reverse order, the database would reject each [DELETE]. All of this occurs in a single transaction: if any one step fails, none of the steps are executed;
  • lines 337–342: a homonym is rejected, unless it is the person currently being edited, who has the right to keep their own first and last names;
  • lines 344–346: A username can belong to only one account.

docs.title: 11.12.5.5. Transactions and uniqueness constraints
docs.text:
• lines 365–375: All updates go through this method. [sessions.begin()] opens a session and its transaction; Upon exiting the [with] block, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]) if everything went well, or rolled back ([ROLLBACK]) if an exception occurs, including [MetierException];
  • Lines 369–370: The optimistic lock detected a concurrent modification (example 28);
  • lines 371–374: a database constraint rejected the write. The checks performed before the write (unique username, no homonyms) provide a clear message in the vast majority of cases; however, two administrators could register the same username at the same time, or two patients could book the same time slot. The uniqueness constraint then rejects the second write, and [SQLAlchemy] releases a [IntegrityError]. Its original message ([e.orig], the error for [PyMySQL]) cites the name of the constraint (here with [MariaDB], for the second time slot booked twice on the same day):
(1062, "Duplicate entry '2026-09-26-2' for key 'unq1_rv'")
  • The regular expression [CONTRAINTE] (line 91) extracts this name. [MySQL] 8 the prefix with the table name (['rv.unq1_rv']), [MariaDB] no: the part [(?:[^'.]*\.)?] accepts this optional prefix ([(?:...)] is a non-capturing group, [?] makes it optional). The dictionary [MESSAGES_CONTRAINTES] (lines 84–88) associates each known constraint with the key of its message. This is why the script SQL names all of its constraints;
  • line 375: any other error is a true anomaly: [raise], with no parameters, rethrows the current exception, which will result in a 500 error page.

Note the structure of all write methods: an internal function [travail], which contains the operations, is passed to [_transaction], which executes it within a transaction and translates the errors. This is equivalent to the annotation ***[@Transactional]*** of *[Spring]*, written in just a few lines: a function is an object like any other, which can be passed as a parameter.

docs.title: 11.13. Authentication
docs.text: The [auth] folder incorporates the mechanisms from Examples 25 through 27, with three differences: the access rule is reversed (everything is prohibited except what is declared public), users are retrieved from the database, and the creation of a customer account is protected by a “pass.”

docs.title: 11.13.1. auth/mots_de_passe.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/mots_de_passe.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Password hashing: bcrypt, 10 rounds, $2b$ version—like the
# hashes used by the SQL script.
#
# bcrypt only takes into account the first 72 OCTETS of a password (one
# accented character takes up two, in UTF-8); the bcrypt library
# will even reject a longer password. Therefore, only these
# 72 bytes, both during creation and verification.
# =========================================================================
import bcrypt


def _octets(mot_de_passe: str) -> bytes:
    return mot_de_passe.encode("utf-8")[:72]


# the hash to be stored in the database: "$2b$10$" + the salt + the result
def hacher(mot_de_passe: str) -> str:
    return bcrypt.hashpw(_octets(mot_de_passe), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=10)).decode("ascii")


# checkpw hashes the entered password with the "salt" contained in the
# stored, then compares the two results
def verifier(mot_de_passe: str, hachage: str) -> bool:
    return bcrypt.checkpw(_octets(mot_de_passe), hachage.encode("ascii"))
  • Lines 15–16: [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password, and version 5 of the library rejects longer passwords (Example 25). Therefore, only these 72 bytes are passed to it, both during creation and verification: a longer password is accepted, but characters beyond the 72nd byte are ignored. An accented character occupies two bytes in [UTF-8];
  • lines 20–21: the hash is stored in text form: [decode("ascii")] converts the bytes returned by [bcrypt] into a string;
  • lines 26–27: verification (example 25). This module is used by authentication and by the business layer (account creation, password change).

docs.title: 11.13.2. auth/utilisateur.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# auth/utilisateur.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What the JWT token contains, and how to read it.
#
# The claims in our tokens (see AuthService.creer_jeton):
#    su  b : the user account ID (JWT convention: "subject"), in plain text
#    login: the login
#    na  me: the display name ("Marie PELISSIER"), for the navigation bar
#    rol e: ADMIN, DOCTOR, or USER
#    iat, exp: token creation and expiration dates
# =========================================================================
from dataclasses import dataclass

from rdvmedecins.entities import Role


# the logged-in user, in a typed format
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UtilisateurConnecte:
    user_id: int
    login: str
    nom: str
    role: Role

     # the user described by the claims of a token that has already been verified; None if
     # a claim is missing or does not have the expected format
    @staticmethod
    def de(claims: dict) -> "UtilisateurConnecte | None":
        try:
            return UtilisateurConnecte(int(claims["sub"]), claims["login"], claims["nom"],
                                       Role(claims["role"]))
        except (KeyError, ValueError, TypeError):
            return None

    @property
    def est_admin(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.ADMIN

    @property
    def est_patient(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.USER
  • lines 20–24: the logged-in user, in a typed form: Example 25 stored the token’s assertion dictionary in [g.utilisateur]; the application stores this object, whose attributes are known to the editor ([g.utilisateur.role]), and whose role is a value from the enumeration [Role];
  • Lines 29–34: Construction based on the assertions of an already verified token. The result type is written in quotation marks (["UtilisateurConnecte | None"]): when [Python] reads the method definition, the class [UtilisateurConnecte] is not yet fully defined, and its name cannot be used directly. A token with a missing assertion ([KeyError]) or an unexpected value ([ValueError]: an unknown role, a [sub] that is not a number) results in [None]: the user is not authenticated;
  • lines 36–42: two properties: the [@property] decorator transforms a method into a computed property, which is used without parentheses: [g.utilisateur.est_admin].

The token contains the account ID ([sub], in text form, as required by the JWT standard), the login, the display name, and the role: everything the navigation bar and access rules need, without having to query the database for every request.

docs.title: 11.13.3. auth/auth_service.py

# =========================================================================
# auth/auth_service.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Authentication logic:
#    - valider_utilisateur(): verifies a username/password pair;
#    - deposer_jeton(      ) : generates the JWT token for a validated user
#                              and stores it in a cookie in the response;
#    - effacer_jeton(      ) : deletes this cookie;
#    - user()          : the user described by the request cookie.
#
# Where does the JWT token travel?
# With a client like JavaScript, the client’s code would store the token
# and added it itself to every request ("Authorization: Bearer
# ..."). A browser that displays ordinary HTML pages does not know
# how to do this: for it to automatically include the token in every request, it
# must be stored in a COOKIE. The settings in this cookie affect
# security:
#    - HttpOnly: the JavaScript on the page cannot read the cookie (an
#      injected script would therefore be unable to steal the token);
#    - SameSite=Lax: the browser does not send the cookie with a PAS value originating
#      from another site (first line of defense against the so-called CSRF attack; the
#      second is the anti-CSRF token for forms; see rdvmedecins/__init__.py);
#    - Secure: in production (HTTPS), the cookie is never transmitted in plain text;
#    - Max-Age: the cookie is deleted when the token expires.
# =========================================================================
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import jwt
from flask import Request, Response

from rdvmedecins.auth.mots_de_passe import verifier
from rdvmedecins.auth.utilisateur import UtilisateurConnecte
from rdvmedecins.entities import User
from rdvmedecins.repositories.user_repository import UserRepository

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
COOKIE_JWT = "rdvmedecins_jwt"


class AuthService:

    def __init__(self, sessions, users: UserRepository, secret: str, duree_secondes: int,
                 cookie_secure: bool):
         # HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: this is clearly stated
         # clearly at startup rather than upon the first login
        if len(secret.encode("utf-8")) < 32:
            raise RuntimeError("JWT_SECRET doit comporter au moins 32 caractères (cf. config.py).")
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._users = users
        self._secret = secret
        self._duree = timedelta(seconds=duree_secondes)
        self._cookie_secure = cookie_secure

     # None if the login does not exist or if the password is incorrect
    def valider_utilisateur(self, login: str, password: str) -> User | None:
        with self._sessions() as session:
            user = self._users.lire_par_login(session, login)
        if user is None or not verifier(password, user.password):
            return None
        return user

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # generates the token JWT from [user] and stores it in a cookie.
     # The token is SIGNÉ (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser
     # can read it (it is not encrypted), but cannot modify it—any
     # modification would invalidate the signature.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def deposer_jeton(self, reponse: Response, user: User):
        maintenant = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        claims = {
            "sub": str(user.id),
            "login": user.login,
            "nom": user.nom,
            "role": user.role.value,
            "iat": maintenant,
            "exp": maintenant + self._duree,
        }
        jeton = jwt.encode(claims, self._secret, algorithm="HS256")
        reponse.set_cookie(COOKIE_JWT, jeton, max_age=self._duree, path="/", httponly=True,
                           samesite="Lax", secure=self._cookie_secure)

     # deletes the cookie: it is re-set, empty, with a lifetime of zero
    @staticmethod
    def effacer_jeton(reponse: Response):
        reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE_JWT, path="/")

     # the token present in the request, whether it is valid or not
    @staticmethod
    def jeton_de(requete: Request) -> str | None:
        return requete.cookies.get(COOKIE_JWT)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # the user identified by the cookie in the request; None if there is no
     # token, or if the token has expired, is forged, or is malformed.
     # jwt.decode verifies the signature; ET verifies the expiration date (claim exp).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def utilisateur(self, requete: Request) -> UtilisateurConnecte | None:
        jeton = self.jeton_de(requete)
        if not jeton:
            return None
        try:
            claims = jwt.decode(jeton, self._secret, algorithms=["HS256"])
        except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
            return None
        return UtilisateurConnecte.de(claims)
  • lines 46–47: a signature key that is too short is flagged when the application starts, rather than on the first login: [create_app] creates the service, and the exception terminates the application with this message;
  • Lines 55–60: Verification of a username and password. The service reads the user via DAO, in a session that remains open only for the duration of this read; password verification ([bcrypt], which is slow) occurs after the session is closed, to avoid maintaining an unnecessary connection to the database;
  • Lines 68–80: the token (example 25) and its cookie, [rdvmedecins_jwt]. [user.role.value]: the enumeration value, the string ["USER"]. The cookie is assigned the attribute [Secure] in production ([COOKIE_SECURE]);
  • lines 84–85: deleting the cookie. This is a static method: it does not require an object and is called on the class ([AuthService.effacer_jeton(reponse)]);
  • lines 97–105: the user identified by the request cookie, or [None].

docs.title: 11.13.4. auth/securite.py
docs.text:
The core of security: authentication of each request and the access rule.

# =========================================================================
# auth/securite.py
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Who can access what, and how the user is authenticated for each
# request (see examples 25 and 26).
#
# For each request, the authenticate function (a before_request from
# the application):
#    1. reads the cookie token, verifies its signature and expiration date,
#       and stores the user in g.utilisateur (None if none exists);
#    2. applies the access rule: TOUTES actions require an
#       who is authenticated, except for those marked @public (login,
#       account creation, language selection) and static files.
#       This is the “everything is prohibited unless explicitly permitted” rule: an action
#       added later—even if you forgot to secure it—is automatically protected.
# Only then does Flask call the action, whose decorator
# @roles_requis(...) checks the role.
#
# Two failure scenarios, two responses tailored to a HTML application:
#    - no authenticated user (no token, expired or forged token)
#      -> redirect to the login page;
#    - insufficient role -> 403 response, for which web/erreurs.py renders a page.
# =========================================================================
from functools import wraps

from flask import abort, current_app, g, redirect, request, url_for

from rdvmedecins.auth.auth_service import AuthService
from rdvmedecins.entities import Role
from rdvmedecins.web.flash import flash_erreur


# the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists: it was
# deleted since the login (either by the patient themselves in another
# tab, or by the ADMIN). This case is treated as an expired session:
# web/erreurs.py deletes the cookie and redirects to the login page.
class SessionInvalide(Exception):
    pass


# a decorator that marks an action as public (see Example 24)
def publique(action):
    action.publique = True
    return action


def enregistrer(app, auth_service: AuthService):

    @app.before_request
    def authentifier():
        g.utilisateur = auth_service.utilisateur(request)
         # no route matches (a 404 page will follow), or a static file
        if request.endpoint is None or request.endpoint == "static":
            return None
        action = current_app.view_functions[request.endpoint]
        if getattr(action, "publique", False) or g.utilisateur is not None:
            return None
         # a response returned by a before_request stops processing:
         # the action is not called
        return vers_login()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# no authenticated user -> login page. If a cookie were
# present, it means its token is no longer valid: the session has expired.
# The cookie is then deleted, and the user is notified via a pop-up message.
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
def vers_login():
    reponse = redirect(url_for("auth.afficher_login"))
    if AuthService.jeton_de(request):
        AuthService.effacer_jeton(reponse)
        flash_erreur("ERRORS.SESSION_EXPIRED")
    return reponse


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# The user’s role must be one of [roles]; otherwise, a 403 response is returned.
# exiger_roles is called from a before_request blueprint (all
# actions in the blueprint, see controllers/personnes.py); roles_requis is
# the decorator for an action (see Example 26).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
def exiger_roles(*roles: Role):
    if g.utilisateur is None:
        raise SessionInvalide()
    if g.utilisateur.role not in roles:
        abort(403)


def roles_requis(*roles: Role):
    def decorateur(action):
        @wraps(action)
        def action_protegee(*args, **kwargs):
            exiger_roles(*roles)
            return action(*args, **kwargs)

        return action_protegee

    return decorateur
  • lines 37–38: an exception for a special case: the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists (the patient deleted it in another tab, or the administrator deleted it). Actions that require the account raise this exception; the error handler treats it as an expired session (see [web/erreurs.py]);
  • lines 42–44: the decorator that marks an action as public (example 24);
  • lines 50–60: the application’s [before_request] function. First, the user is authenticated for all requests, including public requests: the login page must know whether the user is already logged in. Next, the access rule: a request that does not match any route ([request.endpoint is None]: the 404 page will follow) or that requests a static file is allowed; an action marked as public is allowed; an authenticated user is allowed. Otherwise, the function returns a response (redirecting to the login page), which stops processing: the action is not called.

This is the “everything is prohibited unless explicitly permitted” rule: an action added later—even if you forgot to secure it—is automatically secured. Forgetting to include [@publique] on a public action is immediately obvious (the page redirects to the login page); failing to protect a private action is not immediately apparent: the default rule must be the safest. This is also the rule for version [Spring MVC] ([anyRequest().authenticated()]);

  • lines 68–73: the redirect to the login page. If the request contained a token cookie, it means that token is no longer valid (expired or tampered with): the cookie is deleted, and a pop-up message explains to the user that their session has expired (the screenshot of the end-of-session message, shown above);
  • lines 82–86: authorization. The parameter [*roles] accepts any number of roles in a tuple: [exiger_roles(Role.ADMIN, Role.DOCTOR)]. A role missing from the list results in a 403 error. The [g.utilisateur is None] test should never be true (the access rule has already filtered out anonymous visitors), unless [exiger_roles] were called from a public action: this provides an additional layer of security;
  • lines 89–98: the parameter decorator from Example 26, which calls [exiger_roles]. [exiger_roles] can also be used on its own, within the [before_request] of a blueprint, to protect all of its actions at once (see [controllers/personnes.py]).
