docs.text:
# translation/formats.py: dates and amounts, formatted in the language of the request (see Example 16)
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from babel.dates import format_date
from babel.numbers import format_currency
from flask import g


# a date written out in full
def date_longue(jour: date) -> str:
    return format_date(jour, format="full", locale=g.langue)


# an amount in euros
def monnaie(montant: Decimal) -> str:
    return format_currency(montant, "EUR", locale=g.langue)

The filters in Example 16, which this time use [g.langue]. [Babel] accepts a single language ([fr], [en]) as well as a language and a country ([fr_FR]); for [en], it applies U.S. conventions.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Configuration: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 22
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, g, request

from controllers.langue import COOKIE_LANGUE, langue
from controllers.pages import pages
from traduction import formats
from traduction.traducteur import Traducteur

# Bootstrap, used across the examples (see Example 15)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
     # the translation service: the dictionaries, read UNE times at startup
    traducteur = Traducteur(Path(app.root_path) / "i18n")
    app.extensions["traducteur"] = traducteur
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(langue)
    app.register_blueprint(pages)

     # The language of each request: the language specified in the [langue] cookie, or French otherwise
    @app.before_request
    def fixer_langue():
        g.langue = Traducteur.langue(request.cookies.get(COOKIE_LANGUE))

     # in views: {{ t('CLE') }}, {{ day | date_longue }}, {{ price | currency }}
    app.add_template_global(traducteur.traduire, "t")
    app.add_template_filter(formats.date_longue)
    app.add_template_filter(formats.monnaie)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • lines 20–21: the service, created once at startup. [app.root_path] is the application folder (that of [app.py]);
  • Lines 28–30: Before each action, the request language is set to the language of the [langue] cookie if one exists and is supported; otherwise, it defaults to French. [request.cookies] is the dictionary of cookies sent by the browser;
  • line 33: the service’s [traduire] method is made available to views as a global function under a short name, [t] (the second parameter of [add_template_global]). An object method is used like a function: [traducteur.traduire] is a method associated with the object [traducteur].

docs.title: 5.1.5. Language selection: controllers/langue.py
docs.text:
# controllers/langue.py: language selection
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

from flask import Blueprint, abort, redirect, request

from traduction.traducteur import Traducteur

langue = Blueprint("langue", __name__)

COOKIE_LANGUE = "langue"


# GET /language/en: stores the selection in a cookie, then returns to the previous page
@langue.get("/langue/<code>")
def changer(code):
    if code not in Traducteur.LANGUES:
        abort(404)
    reponse = redirect(page_d_origine())
     # the cookie: valid for one year, unreadable by the JavaScript on the page (httponly),
     # never sent with a POST request originating from another site (same-site)
    reponse.set_cookie(COOKIE_LANGUE, code, max_age=365 * 24 * 3600, httponly=True,
                       samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# the page from which the user came (Referer header), of which only the path is retained:
# redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow
# to redirect the user to another site ("open redirect" vulnerability)
def page_d_origine() -> str:
    url = urlsplit(request.headers.get("Referer", ""))
    chemin = url.path
     # "//site.com/..." would be interpreted by the browser as a URL
     # to a AUTRE site: also rejected
    if not chemin.startswith("/") or chemin.startswith("//"):
        return "/"
    return f"{chemin}?{url.query}" if url.query else chemin
  • line 16: an unknown language code: 404;
  • line 18: the action responds with a redirect to the page the user came from: the user is returned to that page, in the new language;
  • Lines 21–22: The response includes a cookie, which the browser will send back with every request. [max_age] is its lifetime, in seconds: one year. [httponly=True] makes it invisible to the [JavaScript] on the page; [samesite="Lax"] prevents the browser from sending it with a POST request originating from another site. Unlike the session cookie (example 20), this cookie is not signed: it’s not a problem if the user modifies it, as the server only accepts supported languages;
  • lines 29–36: the original page is specified by the [Referer] header in the request (the misspelled version, with a single [r], is the one used in the HTTP standard), which the browser populates with the URL from the page that contained the link. But this header comes from the client, which can put anything in it. Blindly redirecting to this address would turn our application into an *open redirect*: a malicious link bearing our domain name could send the user to a malicious site. Therefore, we retain only the path and parameters of URL ([urlsplit] breaks it down into its components), and we reject any path that begins with [//], which the browser would interpret as the address of another site.

docs.title: 5.1.6. Actions: controllers/pages.py
docs.text:
# controllers/pages.py: the actions are not language-aware; they
# provide data; the views translate and format it
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from flask import Blueprint, render_template

pages = Blueprint("pages", __name__)


@dataclass
class Produit:
    nom: str
    prix: Decimal


@pages.get("/")
def accueil():
    return render_template("pages/accueil.html", nom="Marie", aujourdhui=date(2026, 9, 23))


@pages.get("/produits")
def produits():
    return render_template("pages/produits.html", produits=[
        Produit("Clavier", Decimal("25")),
        Produit("Souris", Decimal("12.5")),
        Produit("Écran", Decimal("1149")),
    ])

Actions are language-agnostic: they provide raw data (a name, a date, amounts). Translation and formatting are handled by the views.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Spring MVC] Web Framework” (2026), which itself followed the documents “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework” and “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework” (2026). This document adapts the [Spring MVC] course to the [Python] environment:

  • the [Spring MVC] framework and the [Java] language are replaced by the [Flask] 3.1 framework and the [Python] language (version 3.12 or later);
  • the [Thymeleaf] views are replaced by [Jinja2] views, the view engine from [Flask];
  • the [Bean Validation] validation is replaced by the [Pydantic] library (action parameters) and by the [WTForms] library (HTML forms);
  • [Spring Security] is replaced by a few dozen lines of [Python] written for this purpose, which rely on the libraries [PyJWT] (the JWT tokens) and [bcrypt] (password hashing);
  • ORM, [Hibernate], and [Spring Data JPA] are replaced by ORM and [SQLAlchemy], still based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the structure of the [Spring MVC] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a specific concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in courses [Spring MVC] and [ASP.NET Core MVC]: a reader familiar with one of these courses can compare the frameworks example by example. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of [Spring] or [ASP.NET]. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the [Python] language (functions, classes, dictionaries, modules). A previous course by the author of this one, Introduction to the Python Language and the Flask Web Framework Through Examples (2020), introduces the [Python] language itself, for those who need to learn it first.

docs.title: 1.1. Flask’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives HTTP requests from the browser and returns HTML pages to it. This is the layer that [Flask] helps us write;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (layer [DAO], for [Data Access Object]) reads from and writes to the database. We will use [SQLAlchemy], a ORM ([Object Relational Mapper]) that maps the rows of the tables to the [Python] objects.

The web layer itself follows the [MVC] ([Model – View – Controller]) model:

  • the controller (C) is a set of functions [Python], called actions, each of which processes a type of request (for example, [GET /agenda]). An action reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view;
  • the view (V) is a [Jinja2] file (extension [.html]): a HTML page that contains [{{ ... }}] expressions and [{% ... %}] instructions ([{% if %}], [{% for %}]...), which the [Jinja2] engine replaces with data from the template.

A note on terminology, to avoid confusion: the [Flask] documentation refers to the function that processes a request as a “view function” and to the [Jinja2] file as a “template.” This document uses the terminology from the [MVC] model, as well as that from the [Spring MVC] and [ASP.NET Core MVC] courses: the function that processes a request is an action, the [Jinja2] file that generates the page is a view, and the term “template” refers to the common view from which other pages inherit (Chapter 4).

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a request, such as HTTP or [GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-26];
  • 2: The web server receives the request and passes it to the [Flask] application. During development, this server is [Werkzeug], the library on which [Flask] is built; in production, it will be a server such as [Waitress] or [Gunicorn]. [Werkzeug] compares the requested path to the application’s routes and selects the action responsible for handling this request: this is routing. Before reaching the action, the request may still pass through functions executed for all requests ([before_request]), which we will explore in subsequent chapters;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer; if necessary, the business layer contacts the [DAO] layer, which queries the database [MySQL] via SQL;
  • 4: The action constructs the view’s model M and instructs the [Jinja2] engine to generate the page (function [render_template]);
  • 5: The page HTML generated by the view is the action’s response, which [Flask] returns to the browser.

[Flask] is one of the two most widely used web frameworks in the [Python] world, along with [Django]. Free and open-source, it works anywhere that [Python] works ([Windows], [Linux], [macOS]). It is a micro-framework: its core is intentionally small (routing, requests and responses, sessions, [Jinja2] views), and everything else (form validation, database access, authentication, etc.) is handled by libraries chosen by the developer. Whereas [Spring Boot] configures a coherent set of components on its own, [Flask] lets the developer assemble their own: the application is more transparent, and you can see everything that’s going on inside it. This is, in fact, what makes it a good tool for learning: almost nothing is hidden. [Flask] can create servers that return JSON to a [JavaScript] client ([Angular], [React], [Flutter]...) as it does traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. This document examines this second use case. Two concepts—[Python]—recur on every page: decorators ([@app.get("/")], [@app.before_request]...), which associate a function with a role, and the explicit passing of the objects each function needs, whereas [Spring] injects them automatically.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Python] 3.13 (any version 3.12 or later is suitable). The [Python] installer also provides the [pip] tool, which downloads and installs the libraries, and the [venv] module, which creates virtual environments (we’ll discuss what these are later);
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor, along with the [Python] extension from Microsoft (which also installs the [Pylance] extension, which analyzes the code);
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • the SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one for [Laragon] under [Windows], starting from the chapter on data access, and for the case study.

Unlike [JDK], which does not contain [Spring], [Python] comes with a very comprehensive standard library; but [Flask] and the other libraries in the document are not included: [pip] downloads them from the [PyPI] repository ([Python Package Index]) during installation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day). Each project describes its libraries in a [requirements.txt] file. The following table lists them, along with the versions used:

docs.title: 1.3. Run the case study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to run the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the role of this appointment application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide him with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced the perfect courses [NestJS], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [Spring MVC]. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It’s located in the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder, next to the [exemples] folder:

flask-sept-2026/
├── exemples/
└── rdvmedecins2-flask/

You must have installed [Python] (version 3.12 or later), [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-flask/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. With [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, from the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-flask] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • create the application’s virtual environment and activate it. A virtual environment is a folder (here, [.venv]) that contains a copy of the [Python] interpreter and the libraries for a specific project—and only those libraries: Each project has its own, in the versions that suit it, without interfering with other projects on the computer. In [Windows] (command prompt or terminal of [Visual Studio Code]):
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

and under [Linux] and [macOS]:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
  • Once the environment is activated, the terminal prompt begins with [(.venv)], and the commands [python] and [pip] are those of the environment. Under [Windows], the [PowerShell] terminal sometimes refuses to run the activation script (message: “Script execution is disabled on this system”): The command [Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned], entered once and for all, enables it. [Visual Studio Code] detects the environment and offers to use it for the project: you must accept (you can also select it using the Python command: Select Interpreter, Ctrl-Shift-P); terminals opened afterward activate it automatically;
  • Install the application’s libraries in the virtual environment:
pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Verify the connection to the database. The application connects to [MySQL] on [localhost], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [config.py] file, on the [DB_PASSWORD = ""] line (for example, [DB_PASSWORD = "monMotDePasse"]). To avoid writing a password to a project file, you can also specify it in the environment variable [FLASK_DB_PASSWORD], which takes precedence over the file: [set FLASK_DB_PASSWORD=monMotDePasse] over [Windows] (command prompt), [$env:FLASK_DB_PASSWORD="monMotDePasse"] takes precedence over [PowerShell], [export FLASK_DB_PASSWORD=monMotDePasse] takes precedence over [Linux], and [macOS];
  • launch the application (under [Linux] and [macOS], [python3] if [python] does not exist):
python app.py
  • The application reads the database, then starts the [Flask] development server. The console displays the SQL commands sent to the database (we’ve included only the main ones here), followed by the server messages:
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT medecins.titre, medecins.nom, medecins.prenom, ... FROM medecins LEFT OUTER JOIN users AS users_1 ON users_1.id = medecins.user ORDER BY medecins.nom, medecins.prenom
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT clients.titre, clients.nom, clients.prenom, ... FROM clients LEFT OUTER JOIN users AS users_1 ON users_1.id = clients.user ORDER BY clients.nom, clients.prenom
... INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK
 * Serving Flask app 'rdvmedecins'
 * Debug mode: on
WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment. Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:8081
Press CTRL+C to quit
 * Restarting with stat
 ... (les mêmes ordres SQL)
 * Debugger is active!
 * Debugger PIN: 332-612-699

Each line of [SQLAlchemy] begins with the date and time (replaced here by [...]). It shows that the application has read the list of doctors and clients (the two requests SQL), that the server is listening on port 8081 at the address [127.0.0.1] (i.e., [localhost]), and that it is running in debug mode: the application restarts automatically whenever a [Python] file is modified ([Restarting with stat]: the process monitoring the files restarts the application, which re-reads the database), and an unexpected error displays a debug page (the “PIN” hides this page from the console). The warning reminds you that this server is intended for development, not for production (the case study explains how to use a production server);

  • Open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, each of which uses the username as the password: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

Upon startup, the application reads the database: if [MySQL] is inaccessible, it stops immediately, and the console displays the reason at the end of a long error message (before the line “Background on this error”). If the message is [Can't connect to MySQL server on 'localhost' ([Errno 111] Connection refused)] (or [[WinError 10061]] under [Windows]), it means that [MySQL] has not started; with [Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'], it means the password is incorrect; with [Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'], that the script SQL has not been executed; with [ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flask'], that the virtual environment is not enabled (or that the libraries have not been installed in it); with [Address already in use] (or [Port 8081 is in use by another program]), that port 8081 is already in use (by version [Spring MVC] of the application, for example). The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. Stop the application using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal.

The case study at the end of the document demonstrates how to use the application and then explains each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [exemples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

exemples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routage/
├── ...
├── 28-couches/
├── commun/
│   └── bootstrap/
└── requirements.txt

Each example is a small application ([Flask]) that runs on its own. All examples use the same libraries, described in the file [exemples/requirements.txt]:

# the example libraries: pip install -r requirements.txt
# (the versions used to write and test the examples)
Flask[async]==3.1.3
Flask-WTF==1.3.0
email-validator==2.3.0
pydantic==2.13.5
Babel==2.18.0
PyJWT==2.15.0
bcrypt==5.0.0
SQLAlchemy==2.1.1
PyMySQL[rsa]==1.2.3
  • line 3: [Flask], and what is needed to write asynchronous actions (the additional [[async]], which adds the [asgiref] library; see example 03);
  • lines 4–7: forms, validation, and language-specific formatting;
  • lines 8–9: authentication (Chapter 8);
  • lines 10–11: database access (Chapter 9). The [[rsa]] update to [PyMySQL] adds the [cryptography] library, which is required to connect to a [MySQL] 8 server using a password-protected account.

Each line is in the form [nom==version]: the [==] operator requires exactly this version, the one with which the examples were tested. One could be less strict ([Flask>=3.1]: version 3.1 or later); however, a future version of a library may change its behavior, and a course must be reproducible exactly as written. Lines beginning with [#] are comments.

To run the examples, first create the virtual environment for the examples once and for all in the [exemples] folder (see the case study for details):

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

([source .venv/bin/activate] under [Linux] and [macOS]). The [commun/bootstrap] folder contains the CSS and [Bootstrap] frameworks, shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15).

Almost all of the examples have the same structure. For example, the one in Example 13:

13-premiere-vue/
├── controllers/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── vues.py
├── models/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── page.py
├── templates/
│   └── vues/
│       ├── index.html
│       └── inconnu.html
└── app.py
  • [app.py]: the application’s startup file, which is executed; it builds the application and starts the server (see Example 01);
  • [controllers]: the controllers, i.e., the files containing the actions. This is a package [Python]: a folder containing modules ([.py] files), which can be imported ([from controllers.vues import vues]). The file [__init__.py], which is empty here, turns the folder into a package (it is executed when the package is first imported);
  • [models]: the classes that describe the models (actions and views);
  • [templates]: the views [Jinja2] (from Chapter 4). [Flask] looks for them in this folder, next to the application file;
  • [static] (starting with Example 15): files sent as-is to the browser (style sheets, images, scripts [JavaScript]).

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select “Open in the built-in terminal”), and activate the example’s virtual environment if it isn’t already active ([..\.venv\Scripts\activate] under [Windows], [source ../.venv/bin/activate] under [Linux], and [macOS]: the environment is located in the [exemples] folder, which is the parent of the example folder), and type:

python app.py

All examples listen on port 5000: only one can be run at a time. Stop the server by entering [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. With [macOS], port 5000 is sometimes already occupied by the system’s “AirPlay Receiver” (message [Address already in use]): You can disable it in System Settings / General / AirDrop and Handoff, or change the port in the [app.py] file from the example ([port=5001]).

When you open the [exemples] folder in [Visual Studio Code], the [Python] extension suggests using the [.venv] environment: This allows you to benefit from syntax highlighting, code completion, and error reporting in each file. Each example is launched from its own folder; this is why the imports for an example ([from controllers.vues import vues]) start from that folder. [Pylance], which analyzes the code from the open folder ([exemples]), can then highlight these imports by reporting them as missing: this has no effect on execution. For [Pylance] to find them, simply open the example’s folder itself (File menu / Open Folder). Finally, all examples run in debug mode (see Example 01): a running application restarts automatically, in about one second, as soon as one of its [Python] files is modified and saved.

Examples that use [Bootstrap] find it in the [commun/bootstrap] folder, not in their own folder: this ensures that only one copy of the file exists. Each of these examples calls it using URL and [/bootstrap/...], via a few lines in its [app.py] file. For example, [15-gabarit/app.py]:

# app.py: the application from Example 15
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, request

from controllers.pages import pages

# Bootstrap, shared by the examples: the examples/common/bootstrap folder,
# referenced from the location of the CE file (not from the current folder)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
     # a blueprint without routes, which serves only static files: the
     # BOOTSTRAP folder, under URL/bootstrap/...
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(pages)
  • Line 11: the path to the folder [commun/bootstrap]. [__file__] is the path to the currently running file ([app.py]); [Path(...).resolve()] makes it an absolute path; [.parent] refers to the folder containing it ([15-gabarit]), and [.parent.parent] refers to the parent folder ([exemples]). The operator [/] of an object [Path] adds an element to the path, using the correct separator ([\] under [Windows], [/] elsewhere). The path therefore does not depend on the current folder: the example finds [Bootstrap] no matter where it is launched from;
  • lines 20–21: A blueprint is a group of routes stored in the application (see Example 02). This blueprint has no routes: it is used solely to publish the [commun/bootstrap] folder (parameter [static_folder]) under URL [/bootstrap] (parameter [static_url_path]). A page can thus use the style sheet [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css].

The other lines in this file will be explained in Example 15.

The appendices describe how to install the tools: [Python], [Visual Studio Code] and its extension [Python], [MySQL] with [Laragon], and [curl].

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer (*Data Access Object*): database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few of its details as possible: the web layer is unaware of SQL, and the business layer is unaware of HTML. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

In [Python], database access is organized across several layers:

  • The DB-API standard (PEP 249) defines the common interface for database drivers: open a connection, execute a SQL command, and read rows. For [MySQL] (and [MariaDB]), we use [PyMySQL], a driver written entirely in [Python], which installs without a compiler;
  • [SQLAlchemy] is the most widely used data access library in [Python]. It has two levels. Its core (*Core*) manages connections (including a connection pool, which keeps a few connections open and lends them to queries, since opening a connection is costly) and constructs SQL statements from [Python] expressions, regardless of the SGBD. Its ORM (*Object-Relational Mapper*) maps [Python] classes (the entities) to database tables and transforms the read rows into objects.

This is equivalent to [JDBC], [JPA] and [Hibernate] to [Java], or [Entity Framework Core] to [C#]. The [Flask-SQLAlchemy] extension slightly simplifies the configuration of [SQLAlchemy] in a [Flask] application; we use [SQLAlchemy] directly, which demonstrates what is happening and keeps the business layers and DAO independent of [Flask].

The example requires a running [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]) server: the appendix explains how to install one using [Laragon].

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The database [dbpersonnes] is created by the script SQL. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersonnes.sql

The [database/dbpersonnes.sql] file:

-- Example 28 database: a single table, [personnes]
-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersonnes;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersonnes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersonnes;

CREATE TABLE personnes (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
   -- the row version, incremented by SQLAlchemy with each modification
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  prenom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  nom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
   -- Two people cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_personnes_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO personnes (prenom, nom, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • line 5: the character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without distinguishing between uppercase and lowercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.

  • Line 15: [SQLAlchemy] refers to a base identified by URL. [mysql+pymysql]: the dialect SQL ([MySQL]) and the driver ([PyMySQL]); then the user and their password (here, [root]; without a password, the configuration is [Laragon]), the server, its port, and the database; finally, the settings: [charset=utf8mb4] enables communication between the driver and the server at [UTF-8]. If your server has a password, modify this line, or set the environment variable [FLASK_DATABASE_URL] (example 25);
  • Line 18: At [True], [SQLAlchemy] displays in the console every SQL command sent to the database. This is very informative, and we’ll use it later on.
# app.py: the application from Example 28; the integration of the three layers
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask
from flask_wtf.csrf import CSRFProtect
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

from controllers.personnes import personnes
from dao.personnes_dao import PersonnesDao
from metier.personnes_metier import PersonnesMetier

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.config.from_pyfile("config.py")
    app.config.from_prefixed_env()

     # Database access: the "engine" of SQLAlchemy manages a POOL of connections
     # (connections opened once and then reused from one request to the next).
     # pool_pre_ping: a connection is tested before being reused
    moteur = create_engine(app.config["DATABASE_URL"], echo=app.config["SQL_ECHO"],
                           pool_pre_ping=True)
     # the session factory; expire_on_commit=False: the read objects remain
     # usable after the transaction ends (by the view, in particular)
    sessions = sessionmaker(moteur, expire_on_commit=False)

     # Layer assembly: DAO -> business layer; the web layer only recognizes the business layer
    app.extensions["metier"] = PersonnesMetier(sessions, PersonnesDao())

    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(personnes)
    CSRFProtect(app)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 26–27: The *engine* of [SQLAlchemy] is the object that manages connections to a database and the connection pool. It is created once, at startup; the first connection is opened only upon the first request. [pool_pre_ping=True] checks a connection from the pool before reusing it: a [MySQL] server closes connections that have been inactive for too long, and the application would otherwise receive an error;
  • Line 30: A session of type ORM is the object used to read from and write to entities; it borrows a connection from the pool and tracks the entities it has read to detect changes to them. [sessionmaker] creates a session factory, each call to which will produce a session. By default, at the end of a transaction, the session “expires” the entities (it forgets their values, to read them again the next time they are used). [expire_on_commit=False] prevents this: the entities returned by the business layer remain usable after the transaction, by the view that displays them;
  • line 33: assembling the layers: the business layer receives the session factory and the DAO layer. The web layer will only be aware of the business layer;
  • line 38: Anti-CSRF protection for the entire application (Example 21).

docs.text:
# entities/personne.py: a row in the table [personnes]
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


# the parent class of all entities: SQLAlchemy stores the
# the class-to-table mapping for each of its child classes
class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Personne(Base):
     # the table name
    __tablename__ = "personnes"

     # the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT); SQLAlchemy re-reads
     # its value after each INSERT. Mapped[int]: the Python type of the column
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
     # the optimistic lock: see __mapper_args__ below
    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column()
    prenom: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(30))
    nom: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(30))
    age: Mapped[int]

     # version_id_col: SQLAlchemy increments the version number with each UPDATE, and adds
     # the condition "AND version = <read value>"
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}

    def __init__(self, prenom: str, nom: str, age: int):
        self.prenom = prenom
        self.nom = nom
        self.age = age
  • lines 8–9: All entities in an application inherit from the same base class, derived from [DeclarativeBase]. [SQLAlchemy] stores the description of each entity (its table, its columns) in this class: this is the declarative model;
  • line 14: the table associated with the class;
  • line 18: a column is declared by an attribute annotated with [Mapped[type]]: the column’s type, [Python]. [mapped_column] specifies its characteristics: in this case, the primary key. By default, an integer primary key is generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]): [SQLAlchemy] re-reads its value after each [INSERT];
  • Lines 21–23: [String(30)] specifies the column length (useful if [SQLAlchemy] were to create the table itself). A column with no special characteristics can simply use the annotation ([age]). The type [Mapped[str]] makes the column required ([NOT NULL]); [Mapped[str | None]] would make it optional;
  • line 27: [version_id_col] designates the version column: [SQLAlchemy] increments it with each [UPDATE], and adds the condition [AND version = <la valeur lue>] to it. If another query has modified the row in the meantime, its version has changed; [UPDATE] does not modify any rows, and [SQLAlchemy] throws a [StaleDataError] exception. This is an optimistic lock: nothing is blocked, but concurrent modifications are detected;
  • Lines 29–32: a constructor to create a person in a single line.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
# dao/personnes_dao.py: the DAO layer, requests, no business rules.
# Each method receives the SESSION from SQLAlchemy, opened by the layer
# business layer: all requests for the same operation thus share the same
# connection and the same transaction
from sqlalchemy import delete, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from entities.personne import Personne


class PersonnesDao:

     # SELECT ... FROM people ORDER BY last name, first name
    def lister(self, session: Session) -> list[Personne]:
        return list(session.scalars(select(Personne).order_by(Personne.nom, Personne.prenom)))

     # SELECT ... WHERE id = ?; None if the person does not exist
    def lire(self, session: Session, id: int) -> Personne | None:
        return session.get(Personne, id)

     # a person with the same first and last name, other than [sauf_id]:
     # SELECT ... WHERE first_name = ? AND last_name = ? AND id <> ? LIMIT 1
    def homonyme(self, session: Session, prenom: str, nom: str, sauf_id: int = 0) -> Personne | None:
        requete = select(Personne).where(Personne.prenom == prenom, Personne.nom == nom,
                                         Personne.id != sauf_id).limit(1)
        return session.scalars(requete).first()

     # INSERT (new person): the person is added to the session, and
     # flush sends TOUT DE SUITE the command SQL (not to COMMIT)
    def ajouter(self, session: Session, personne: Personne) -> Personne:
        session.add(personne)
        session.flush()
        return personne

     # DELETE FROM people WHERE id = ?
    def supprimer(self, session: Session, id: int):
        session.execute(delete(Personne).where(Personne.id == id))

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business rules. Each method receives the session opened by the business layer: all queries for a single business operation thus share the same connection and the same transaction.

  • Line 15: [select(Personne)] constructs a query ([SELECT]) on the "people" table; [order_by] sorts it. The columns are written as attributes of the class ([Personne.nom]): the editor can verify their names, and no SQL is written by hand. [session.scalars(...)] executes the query and returns the entities constructed from the read rows;
  • line 19: reading by primary key, or [None];
  • lines 23–26: [where] adds conditions, written using the operators from [Python] ([==], [!=]): [SQLAlchemy] translates them into SQL, with parameters (the values are never copied into the text of the SQL command, which makes SQL injection impossible). [first()] returns the first entity, or [None];
  • lines 30–33: [session.add] assigns a new entity to the session; [flush] immediately sends [INSERT] to the database (without [flush], it would go to [COMMIT]). The database then generates the ID, which [SQLAlchemy] stores in the entity;
  • line 37: a [DELETE], constructed in the same way.

docs.text:
# occupation/donnees.py: a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DonneesPersonne:
    prenom: str
    nom: str
    age: int

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Flask], [WTForms], or [SQLAlchemy].

# business/exception.py: a business rule rejects the operation; the message
# is intended for the user
class MetierException(Exception):
    pass

An exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user.

# business/personnes_metier.py: the MÉTIER layer and the business rules—and only those.
# Each method opens its own TRANSACTION: validated (COMMIT) at the end of the block
# with, rolled back (ROLLBACK) if an exception occurs
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import StaleDataError

from dao.personnes_dao import PersonnesDao
from entities.personne import Personne
from metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne
from metier.exception import MetierException

HOMONYME = "Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom."
MODIFIEE = "Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps : rechargez-la."
INCONNUE = "Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus)."


class PersonnesMetier:

     # sessions: the session "factory" SQLAlchemy (see app.py)
    def __init__(self, sessions: sessionmaker, dao: PersonnesDao):
        self._sessions = sessions
        self._dao = dao

    def lister(self) -> list[Personne]:
         # sessions.begin(): a session ET commits its transaction; the `with` block closes them
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            return self._dao.lister(session)

    def lire(self, id: int) -> Personne:
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            return self._lire(session, id)

    def ajouter(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                 # Rule 1: No two people can have the same first and last names
                if self._dao.homonyme(session, donnees.prenom, donnees.nom):
                    raise MetierException(HOMONYME)
                return self._dao.ajouter(session, Personne(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, donnees.age))
        except IntegrityError as e:
            raise self._traduire(e)

    def modifier(self, id: int, version: int | None, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
        try:
            with self._sessions.begin() as session:
                personne = self._lire(session, id)
                 # Rule 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else
                if personne.version != version:
                    raise MetierException(MODIFIEE)
                if self._dao.homonyme(session, donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, id):
                    raise MetierException(HOMONYME)
                 # The entity being read is “tracked” by the session: simply
                 # modify it; `flush` sends the UPDATE immediately
                personne.prenom = donnees.prenom
                personne.nom = donnees.nom
                personne.age = donnees.age
                session.flush()
                return personne
        except StaleDataError:
             # the UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." did not modify any rows
            raise MetierException(MODIFIEE)
        except IntegrityError as e:
            raise self._traduire(e)

    def supprimer(self, id: int) -> Personne:
        with self._sessions.begin() as session:
            personne = self._lire(session, id)
            self._dao.supprimer(session, id)
            return personne

    def _lire(self, session, id: int) -> Personne:
        personne = self._dao.lire(session, id)
        if personne is None:
            raise MetierException(INCONNUE)
        return personne

     # two simultaneous insertions: the database’s uniqueness constraint rejected the
     # second one; e.orig: the original error, the one from the driver PyMySQL
    @staticmethod
    def _traduire(e: IntegrityError) -> Exception:
        if "unq_personnes_prenom_nom" in str(e.orig):
            return MetierException(HOMONYME)
        return e
  • Line 27: Each method opens its own session and transaction: [sessions.begin()] returns a session with a transaction that has been started. At the end of the [with] block, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]) and the session is closed; if an exception occurs within the block, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the block are retained. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation equals one transaction;
  • lines 34–42: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The business layer checks this rule before writing to the database and raises a [MetierException] if it is not met. But this check is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there are no namesakes, and then both proceed to insert the data. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and [SQLAlchemy] triggers a [IntegrityError], which the [_traduire] method transforms into the same [MetierException]. The database is the last line of defense;
  • lines 44–64: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. Here again, the database (via the optimistic lock) detects cases where a concurrent modification occurs between the read and the [UPDATE]: this is the [StaleDataError] exception. Note that the modification is performed simply by changing the attributes of the read entity: the session tracks this, and [flush] sends a [UPDATE] containing only the modified columns;
  • lines 66–70: Deleting a person results in the confirmation message;
  • lines 72–76: A nonexistent person is a business error;
  • lines 80–84: A static method does not accept either an object or a class; it is simply a function defined within the class. [e.orig] is the original exception, that of the driver [PyMySQL], whose message contains the name of the violated constraint. Another integrity error is reported as-is: this is not a business error, but a programming error.

docs.text:
# models/formulaire_personne.py: the form fields and their constraints (see Example 19)
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import HiddenField, IntegerField, StringField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, InputRequired, Length, NumberRange, Optional


def nettoyer(valeur):
    return valeur.strip() if isinstance(valeur, str) else valeur


# a version: an integer, or None if the field is empty (add form)
def entier_ou_none(valeur):
    return int(valeur) if valeur not in (None, "") else None


class PersonneForm(FlaskForm):

    class Meta:
        locales = ["fr"]

    prenom = StringField("Prénom", filters=[nettoyer], validators=[
        DataRequired("Le prénom est obligatoire."), Length(max=30, message="30 caractères au plus.")])
    nom = StringField("Nom", filters=[nettoyer], validators=[
        DataRequired("Le nom est obligatoire."), Length(max=30, message="30 caractères au plus.")])
    age = IntegerField("Âge", validators=[
        InputRequired("L'âge est obligatoire."),
        NumberRange(min=0, max=150, message="L'âge doit être compris entre 0 et 150.")])
     # the record’s version, carried by a hidden field (update only)
    version = HiddenField(filters=[entier_ou_none])

The form [WTForms] (Example 19). The hidden field [version] has a filter that converts it to an integer, or to [None] if it is empty (add form).

# controllers/personnes.py: the WEB layer; it only interacts with the business layer
from flask import Blueprint, current_app, flash, redirect, render_template, url_for

from metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne
from metier.exception import MetierException
from metier.personnes_metier import PersonnesMetier
from models.formulaire_personne import PersonneForm

personnes = Blueprint("personnes", __name__)


def metier() -> PersonnesMetier:
    return current_app.extensions["metier"]


@personnes.get("/")
def accueil():
    return redirect(url_for("personnes.liste"))


@personnes.get("/personnes")
def liste():
    return render_template("personnes/liste.html", personnes=metier().lister())


@personnes.get("/personnes/ajout")
def ajout():
    return formulaire("Ajouter une personne", url_for("personnes.ajouter"), PersonneForm())


@personnes.post("/personnes/ajout")
def ajouter():
    form = PersonneForm()
    if not form.validate():
        return formulaire("Ajouter une personne", url_for("personnes.ajouter"), form)
    try:
        p = metier().ajouter(DonneesPersonne(form.prenom.data, form.nom.data, form.age.data))
    except MetierException as e:
         # A business rule rejects the data: the form is redisplayed, along with the message at the bottom of the page
        return formulaire("Ajouter une personne", url_for("personnes.ajouter"), form, str(e))
    flash(f"{p.prenom} {p.nom} a été ajouté(e).", "succes")
    return redirect(url_for("personnes.liste"))


@personnes.get("/personnes/<int:id>/modification")
def modification(id):
    try:
        p = metier().lire(id)
    except MetierException as e:
        flash(str(e), "erreur")
        return redirect(url_for("personnes.liste"))
     # obj=p: the form fields are populated with the attributes of the same name as those in p
    return formulaire("Modifier une personne", url_for("personnes.modifier", id=id),
                      PersonneForm(obj=p))


@personnes.post("/personnes/<int:id>/modification")
def modifier(id):
    action = url_for("personnes.modifier", id=id)
    form = PersonneForm()
    if not form.validate():
        return formulaire("Modifier une personne", action, form)
    try:
        donnees = DonneesPersonne(form.prenom.data, form.nom.data, form.age.data)
        p = metier().modifier(id, form.version.data, donnees)
    except MetierException as e:
        return formulaire("Modifier une personne", action, form, str(e))
    flash(f"{p.prenom} {p.nom} a été modifié(e).", "succes")
    return redirect(url_for("personnes.liste"))


@personnes.post("/personnes/<int:id>/suppression")
def supprimer(id):
    try:
        p = metier().supprimer(id)
        flash(f"{p.prenom} {p.nom} a été supprimé(e).", "succes")
    except MetierException as e:
         # no form to redisplay: the error is also displayed as a flash message
        flash(str(e), "erreur")
    return redirect(url_for("personnes.liste"))


# the form page: title, shipping address, form, global error
def formulaire(titre: str, action: str, form: PersonneForm, erreur: str | None = None):
    return render_template("personnes/formulaire.html", titre=titre, action=action,
                           form=form, erreur=erreur)
  • lines 12–13: the business layer, the only layer known to the controller;
  • lines 32–18: the add operation, in three steps: form validation (input errors), calling the business layer (business rules), then the PRG schema. A [MetierException] re-displays the form, along with its footer message. [flash] receives a category as its second parameter (["succes"]), which the template uses to select the message’s presentation;
  • lines 46–54: the edit form, pre-filled: the parameter [obj] fills the form fields with the object’s attributes of the same name, including the version. A nonexistent person redirects to the list, with a flashing error message;
  • lines 58–42: the edit, following the same pattern as the add operation;
  • lines 73–51: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any error is also displayed in a pop-up message, of category ["erreur"].

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Personnes</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('bootstrap.static', filename='css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# success messages (flash messages in the "success" category): at the top #}

    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}

  </div>
  {% include "fragments/confirmation.html" %}

</html>
  • lines 12–14: [category_filter] renders only the flash messages of the specified categories: success messages, at the top of the page;
  • lines 19–21: errors, at the bottom of the page: those occurring before a redirect (flash messages), followed by the error from the current request (variable [erreur]). The operator [+] concatenates two lists.
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Personnes</h1>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <thead><tr><th>Prénom</th><th>Nom</th><th>Âge</th><th></th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for p in personnes %}
      <tr>
        <td>{{ p.prenom }}</td>
        <td>{{ p.nom }}</td>
        <td>{{ p.age }}</td>
        <td class="text-end">
          <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" href="{{ url_for('personnes.modification', id=p.id) }}">Modifier</a>
          <form method="post" class="d-inline" action="{{ url_for('personnes.supprimer', id=p.id) }}"
                data-confirmation="Supprimer {{ p.prenom }} {{ p.nom }} ?">
            <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token() }}">
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Supprimer</button>
          </form>
        </td>
      </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  <a class="btn btn-primary" href="{{ url_for('personnes.ajout') }}">Ajouter une personne</a>
{% endblock %}

The list includes the links and buttons from Example 21, along with its confirmation window (the files [fragments/confirmation.html] and [static/js/app.js] are those from Example 21).

docs.title: 9.1.8. The commands SQL
docs.text:
Let’s restart the application with the environment variable [FLASK_SQL_ECHO=true] (under [Windows]: [$env:FLASK_SQL_ECHO="true"]), and monitor the SQL commands for a modification in the console. The display of the change form for person No. 1:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT personnes.id, personnes.version, personnes.prenom, personnes.nom, personnes.age
FROM personnes
WHERE personnes.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00017s] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine COMMIT

A transaction, [SELECT], per primary key, whose value is passed as a parameter ([%(pk_1)s]; see the parameter syntax for [PyMySQL]). Saving the master record with a new age:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT personnes.id, personnes.version, personnes.prenom, personnes.nom, personnes.age
FROM personnes
WHERE personnes.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [cached since 0.05972s ago] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT personnes.id, personnes.version, personnes.prenom, personnes.nom, personnes.age
FROM personnes
WHERE personnes.prenom = %(prenom_1)s AND personnes.nom = %(nom_1)s AND personnes.id != %(id_1)s
 LIMIT %(param_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00016s] {'prenom_1': 'Marie', 'nom_1': 'Pélissier', 'id_1': 1, 'param_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine UPDATE personnes SET version=%(version)s, age=%(age)s WHERE personnes.id = %(personnes_id)s AND personnes.version = %(personnes_version)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00015s] {'version': 1, 'age': 43, 'personnes_id': 1, 'personnes_version': 0}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine COMMIT

In a single transaction, we can see the following: reading the record, searching for a namesake, and then the [UPDATE]. This transaction modifies only the changed column ([age]), increments the version (from 0 to 1), and sets the optimistic lock condition ([AND personnes.version = 0]). The entry [cached since] indicates that [SQLAlchemy] reused the translation in SQL from a previously constructed request. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still with version 0:

INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine BEGIN (implicit)
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT personnes.id, personnes.version, personnes.prenom, personnes.nom, personnes.age
FROM personnes
WHERE personnes.id = %(pk_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [cached since 0.09593s ago] {'pk_1': 1}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine ROLLBACK

The version being read (1) is not the same as the form’s version (0): the business layer raised a [MetierException], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified in the meantime: please reload it.” Similarly, the process of adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 3. The Action Template
docs.text:
An action requires information sent by the browser: the parameters of the URL ([?nom=martin&age=42]), form fields, the request body JSON, and sometimes a request header HTTP. The original course refers to all of this information as the action model. This chapter shows how an action retrieves this information, converts it to the correct type, and validates it. This process is called data binding.

[Flask] is much more minimalist here than other frameworks: it provides access to the request information in the form of character strings and stops there. Converting ["42"] to the integer 42, verifying that a name has at least two characters, and assembling the fields into an object—all of this is the responsibility of the application. We’ll first do this by hand (Example 07), then using the [Pydantic] library (Examples 08–12), which describes a model using a class in which each field specifies its type and constraints. In the next chapter, the HTML forms will be handled by another library, [WTForms], designed specifically for them; [Pydantic] remains the natural tool for the parameters of a URL and for the JSON bodies of the API.

Note on terminology: In the following chapter, the word “model” will primarily refer to the data that an action transmits to its view. The model of an action, as used in this chapter, is what it receives.

Examples 07 through 12 are run in the same way as those in the previous chapter: open a terminal to the example directory, with the virtual environment activated ([python app.py]); [Ctrl-C] stops the server. Their [app.py] files are all similar: a factory [create_app] that creates the application, configures the provider JSON (accents preserved, keys in their original order; see Example 03), and saves a blueprint. We’ll only comment on them when they introduce something new.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: The parameters of URL
docs.text:
The parameters for URL are the portion that follows [?]: [?nom=martin&age=42]. This portion is called the query string (*query string*). Each parameter is a pair of [nom=valeur]; the pairs are separated by [&]. The [controllers/parametres.py] file:

# controllers/parametres.py: the parameters of URL (the "query string")
from flask import Blueprint, abort, request

parametres = Blueprint("parametres", __name__, url_prefix="/parametres")


# /settings/action01?name=martin: request.args contains the parameters for
# the URL; `get` returns the parameter’s value, or `None` if it is absent
@parametres.get("/action01")
def action01():
    nom = request.args.get("nom")
    return f"nom = [{nom}], de type {type(nom).__name__}"


# /parameters/action02?age=42: type=int CONVERTIT the value (a string) in
# integer; a missing parameter, or one that is not an integer, returns None
@parametres.get("/action02")
def action02():
    age = request.args.get("age", type=int)
    return f"age = [{age}], de type {type(age).__name__}"


# /parameters/action03?age=42: a parameter OBLIGATOIRE; its absence, or a
# value that is not an integer causes the action to terminate with a 400 (Bad Request) response
@parametres.get("/action03")
def action03():
    texte = request.args.get("age")
    if texte is None:
         # "abort" raises an exception, which Flask converts into an error response
        abort(400, "le paramètre [age] est obligatoire")
     # we are responsible for the conversion
    try:
        age = int(texte)
    except ValueError:
        abort(400, f"[{texte}] n'est pas un nombre entier")
    return f"age = [{age}], de type {type(age).__name__}"


# /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
@parametres.get("/action04")
def action04():
    page = request.args.get("page", default=1, type=int)
    return f"page = [{page}]"


# /parameters/action05?q=flask: the parameter name in URL is not necessarily
# the same as the Python variable
@parametres.get("/action05")
def action05():
    recherche = request.args.get("q")
    return f"recherche = [{recherche}]"


# /settings/action06?name=martin&age=42: all parameters at once, in a dictionary
@parametres.get("/action06")
def action06():
    return request.args.to_dict()
  • line 11: [request.args] contains the parameters of URL, which have already been decoded by [Werkzeug]. This is a special dictionary, a [MultiDict], which, as we’ll see in Example 10, accepts multiple values per key. Its method [get] returns the value of a parameter, or [None] if it is absent. Unlike [request.args["nom"]], which would throw an exception for a missing parameter, [get] never causes an error;
  • line 12: the action displays the value and its type: [type(x)] is the class of [x], and [__name__] is the name of that class. A value retrieved from URL is always a string ([str]);
  • line 19: the parameter [type] of [get] specifies a conversion function applied to the string: in this case, [int], the class of integers, whose call to [int("42")] returns 42. If the conversion fails ([int("abc")] raises a [ValueError]), [get] returns [None], just as it would for a missing parameter: the action cannot distinguish between the two cases, and the input error goes unnoticed;
  • Lines 26–35: a required parameter and a manual conversion that distinguishes between the two possible errors. [abort(400, message)] terminates the action with a 400 response (*Bad Request*—the request is invalid), accompanied by the message (see Example 03). The statement [try] / [except ValueError] catches the exception thrown by [int];
  • line 42: a default value, used if the parameter is missing (or if its conversion fails). This is a typical case for a page number in a list;
  • line 50: there is no requirement to name the variable [Python] the same as the parameter of URL. Search engines often use a short parameter, [q] (*query*);
  • line 57: [to_dict()] converts [MultiDict] into a standard [Python] dictionary (by retaining only the first value of each parameter), which the action returns as: [Flask] transforms it into JSON (see Example 03).

Let’s test each action with [curl]. A parameter is present, then absent:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action01?nom=martin"
curl http://localhost:5000/settings/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 27

nom = [martin], de type str
nom = [None], de type NoneType

The quotation marks around URL are necessary in a terminal: without them, the shell would interpret [&] (which runs a command in the background under [Linux]) and [?]. A value containing spaces or special characters must be encoded in the URL: a space becomes [%20], and [&] becomes [%26] (otherwise, it would separate two parameters). The browser handles this automatically; with [curl], you have to write it out. [Werkzeug] decodes the value before storing it in [request.args]:

curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action01?nom=jean%20dupont%20%26%20fils"

nom = [jean dupont & fils], de type str

The conversion using [type=int], which was successful at first but then failed:

curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action02?age=42"
curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action02?age=abc"

age = [42], de type int
age = [None], de type NoneType

The required parameter for action 03, missing and then invalid:

curl -i http://localhost:5000/settings/action03
curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 126

<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>le paramètre [age] est obligatoire</p>
<!doctype html>
<html lang=en>
<title>400 Bad Request</title>
<h1>Bad Request</h1>
<p>[abc] n&#39 is not an integer</p>

The default value and the renamed parameter:

curl http://localhost:5000/settings/action04
curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action04?page=3"
curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action05?q=flask"

page = [1]
page = [3]
recherche = [flask]

Finally, all parameters at once. The parameter [nom] appears twice: [to_dict()] retains only the first value.

curl "http://localhost:5000/parametres/action06?nom=martin&age=42&nom=durand"

{
  "nom": "martin",
  "age": "42"
}

The age remained a string (["42"], enclosed in quotes in JSON): no conversion was requested. In a browser (here [Chromium]), JSON appears on a single line: [Flask] only indents JSON in debug mode, and the screenshot was taken without it; the “Pretty-print” checkbox would display it indented. Incidentally, the address bar shows the encoding of accented characters in URL ([é] becomes [%C3%A9], with its two bytes in [UTF-8]):

This first example illustrates the limitations of the manual approach: for each parameter, you must write the reading, conversion, and handling of missing values and errors. With ten parameters, the action’s code would be overwhelmed by these checks. It is better to describe what is expected and let a library handle the verification. That is the purpose of the following example.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action model described by a class
docs.text: [Pydantic] is the most widely used data validation library in [Python] (it is at the core of the [FastAPI] framework). It describes the data expected by a class: each attribute has a type and, optionally, constraints. [Pydantic] is responsible for converting the received data into these types and for validating the constraints. It is installed in the example’s virtual environment (file [requirements.txt]).

docs.title: 3.2.1. The model: models/personne.py
docs.text:
# models/personne.py: the action model, a PyDantic class in which each
# field has its own type and constraints
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, EmailStr, Field


class PersonneModele(BaseModel):
     # the received strings are stripped of any surrounding spaces
    model_config = ConfigDict(str_strip_whitespace=True)

     # required (no default value), 2 to 20 characters
    nom: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=2, max_length=20)]
     # an integer ("42" is converted to 42), between 0 and 150
    age: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=150)]
     # only one of these three values
    titre: Literal["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]
     # optional (default is None); if present, a valid email address
    email: EmailStr | None = None
  • Line 8: A [Pydantic] model is a class that inherits from [BaseModel]. Its attributes are declared at the class level, along with their types, as in a [dataclass] (Example 06);
  • Line 10: The model’s configuration. [str_strip_whitespace=True] removes the spaces surrounding the received strings: a name entered as [" martin "] becomes ["martin"] before being validated. The attribute [model_config] is not a field in the template: [Pydantic] recognizes this reserved name;
  • Line 13: the field [nom]. [Annotated[str, Field(...)]] reads “the type [str], annotated by [Field(...)].” [Annotated], from the standard module [typing], allows additional information to be attached to a type—information that [Python] ignores but that the libraries read: here, the constraints of [Pydantic], a length of 2 to 20 characters ([min_length], [max_length]). The field has no default value: it is required;
  • line 15: the type [int]: [Pydantic] converts the string ["42"] to the integer 42, and rejects ["abc"]. The constraints [ge] (*greater or equal*) and [le] (*less or equal*) limit the value. There are also [gt] and [lt] for strict inequalities;
  • line 17: [Literal["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]] is the type of the three values listed, and only those;
  • line 19: [EmailStr] is the type of an email address; [Pydantic] validates its syntax using the [email-validator] library (which is also installed by [requirements.txt]). [EmailStr | None]: an address, or [None]. The default value [= None] makes the field optional.

This template describes the expected data; it contains no validation instructions. This is known as a declarative style.

docs.title: 3.2.2. The action: controllers/personnes.py
docs.text:
# controllers/personnes.py: an action whose model is a Pydantic class
from flask import Blueprint, request

from models.personne import PersonneModele

personnes = Blueprint("personnes", __name__, url_prefix="/personnes")


# /people/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
# model_validate: Pydantic creates the object from the parameter dictionary
# (LIAISON: converts strings to the type of each field), then checks
# the constraints (VALIDATION). An invalid model raises a ValidationError,
# which is converted to a 400 response by app.py: the process stops there
@personnes.get("/action01")
def action01():
    personne = PersonneModele.model_validate(request.args.to_dict())
    return {
         # model_dump: the object in dictionary form (serializable as JSON)
        "personne": personne.model_dump(),
        "typeAge": type(personne.age).__name__,
    }
  • Line 16: The [model_validate] class method creates a [PersonneModele] object from a dictionary—in this case, the one containing the parameters of URL. It performs two actions, in this order: - binding: each value in the dictionary is assigned to the field of the same name, after being converted to the field’s type (["42"] → 42); - validation: the constraints for each field are checked (length, bounds, allowed values, etc.).
  • If either step fails, [model_validate] throws a [ValidationError] exception, which contains a list of all errors (not just the first one). The action does not handle it: it stops; we’ll see who takes care of it;
  • line 19: [model_dump()] returns the object as a dictionary, which [Flask] can convert to JSON;
  • line 20: the age type, to show that the conversion took place.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Error handling: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 08
from flask import Flask
from pydantic import ValidationError

from controllers.personnes import personnes


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
     # JSON: accents preserved, keys in their original order (see Example 03)
    app.json.ensure_ascii = False
    app.json.sort_keys = False
    app.register_blueprint(personnes)

     # an invalid template: the Pydantic exception ValidationError becomes,
     # for TOUTE the application, a 400 response detailing the errors
    @app.errorhandler(ValidationError)
    def modele_invalide(e: ValidationError):
        erreurs = [{"champ": ".".join(str(x) for x in err["loc"]), "message": err["msg"]}
                   for err in e.errors()]
        return {"statut": 400, "erreurs": erreurs}, 400

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 17–21: The decorator [@app.errorhandler(ValidationError)] registers an exception handler: when an action throws a [ValidationError] (or an exception of a derived class), [Flask] calls this function, passing the exception as a parameter, and returns its return value as the response. Declared at the application level, the handler applies to all of its actions: every action that validates a model benefits from it, without having to write a single line of error-handling code;
  • Line 19: [e.errors()] returns the list of errors. Each error is a dictionary; We retain two pieces of information: [loc] (*location*), the affected field, in the form of a tuple ([("nom",)]; see Example 10 for a longer tuple), and [msg], the message. The expression [[... for err in e.errors()]] is a list comprehension: it constructs a list by applying the expression on the left to each element;
  • line 21: a tuple [(corps, code)] (see Example 03): a dictionary, converted to JSON, and the code 400.

docs.title: 3.2.4. Execution
docs.text:
A valid template:

curl -i "http://localhost:5000/personnes/action01?nom=martin&age=42&titre=Mr"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 117

{
  "personne": {
    "nom": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "titre": "Mr",
    "email": null

curl "http://localhost:5000/personnes/action01?nom=%20%20martin%20&age=42&titre=Mme&email=martin@exemple.fr"

{

    "nom": "martin",
    "age": 42,
    "titre": "Mme",
    "email": "martin@exemple.fr"
  },

No parameters: the three required fields are missing.

curl -i http://localhost:5000/people/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 BAD REQUEST
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 248

{
  "statut": 400,
  "erreurs": [
    {
      "champ": "nom",
      "message": "Field required"
    },
    {
      "champ": "age",
      "message": "Field required"
    },
    {
      "champ": "titre",
      "message": "Field required"
    }
