docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 16
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask, g, request

from aides import formats
from controllers.pages import pages

BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(pages)

     # the formatting language for each request: the ?lang=en parameter in URL,
     # French otherwise. before_request: a function executed before the CHAQUE
     # action; [g]: an object that exists for the duration of a request
    @app.before_request
    def fixer_langue():
        g.locale = "en_US" if request.args.get("lang") == "en" else "fr_FR"

     # "home" FILTRES: {{ price | currency }}, {{ day | date_longue }}
    app.add_template_filter(formats.monnaie)
    app.add_template_filter(formats.date_longue)
     # a global FONCTION, callable in all views: {{ uppercase(name) }}
    app.add_template_global(formats.majuscules)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • Lines 23–25: The formatting language depends on the request: the parameter [?lang=en] of URL selects English; French is the default language. [@app.before_request] registers a function that [Flask] executes before each action (the chapter on the request lifecycle will detail these “hooks”). It stores the locale in [g], an object of [Flask] which, like [request], is specific to the current query: you can store whatever you want in it ([g.locale = ...]); it is discarded at the end of the query. This is the way to share information between the different functions that process the same query, without passing it as a parameter from one to the next. The chapter on data scopes will revisit this topic;
  • lines 28–29: registering two functions as filters—[Jinja2]—under their names. A filter receives as its first parameter the value placed before [|]; the subsequent parameters are those of the filter: [{{ prix | monnaie("USD") }}] calls [monnaie(prix, "USD")];
  • Line 31: Registering a function as a global view function.

The decorator [@app.template_filter()] (applied to the function itself) is another way to register a filter. Calling [add_template_filter] from within [app.py] has the advantage of keeping the module [aides/formats.py] independent of [Flask] (with the exception of [g]).

docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: A GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form sends its fields to the server in one of two ways, depending on its [method] attribute:

  • [method="get"]: The fields are added to the URL as parameters ([/recherche?motCle=le&genre=roman]). This is the method used by a form that performs a query: a search or a filter. The URL containing the results can be bookmarked, shared, or reloaded safely;
  • [method="post"]: The fields are included in the request body (see Example 11). This is the method used by a form that modifies data: a registration, an addition, or a deletion.

This first form is a book search.

docs.title: 4.5.1. The model: models/livres.py
docs.text:
# models/livres.py: a book, and the view template
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Livre:
    titre: str
    auteur: str
    genre: str


# the view template: the input field (to redisplay it), genres, results
@dataclass
class RechercheModele:
    mot_cle: str
    genre: str
    genres: list[str]
    resultats: list[Livre]
  • Line 5: [frozen=True] makes the [Livre] objects immutable: once created, their attributes can no longer be modified. This is a good practice for data shared by all requests, such as the list of books;
  • lines 14–18: The view model contains the user’s input—so the form can display it again—the list of suggested genres, and the results.

docs.title: 4.5.2. The controller: controllers/livres.py
docs.text:
# controllers/livres.py: a search form, submitted by GET
from flask import Blueprint, render_template, request

from models.livres import Livre, RechercheModele

livres = Blueprint("livres", __name__)

LIVRES = (
    Livre("Le Rouge et le Noir", "Stendhal", "roman"),
    Livre("Les Fleurs du mal", "Baudelaire", "poésie"),
    Livre("Madame Bovary", "Flaubert", "roman"),
    Livre("Alcools", "Apollinaire", "poésie"),
    Livre("Le Cid", "Corneille", "théâtre"),
)

GENRES = ["roman", "poésie", "théâtre"]


# GET / and GET/search?motCle=...&genre=...: the ET form and its results.
# Two decorators: two paths to the same action
@livres.get("/")
@livres.get("/recherche")
def recherche():
    mot_cle = request.args.get("motCle", "")
    genre = request.args.get("genre", "")
    mot = mot_cle.strip().lower()
    resultats = [livre for livre in LIVRES
                 if (not mot or mot in livre.titre.lower() or mot in livre.auteur.lower())
                 and (not genre or livre.genre == genre)]
    return render_template("livres/recherche.html",
                           modele=RechercheModele(mot_cle, genre, GENRES, resultats))
  • lines 8–16: the data, hard-coded for this example. [LIVRES] is a tuple (enclosed in parentheses), an immutable sequence. By convention, uppercase names indicate constants;
  • lines 21–22: two route decorators on the same action: it responds to both URL. On the first visit ([/]), there are no parameters: all books are displayed;
  • lines 24–25: The form fields are read as parameters for URL (example 07). The second parameter of [get] is the default value;
  • lines 27–29: filtering using a list comprehension with a condition ([if]): a book is selected if the keyword is empty or appears in its title or author (in lowercase on both sides), and if the genre is empty or matches the book’s genre;
  • line 31: the view template.

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Recherche de livres</h1>
  {# method="get": the fields are sent in the URL (?motCle=...&genre=...) #}
  <form method="get" action="/recherche" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="motCle">Titre ou auteur</label>
      {# value: the field displays the entered value (escaped by {{ }}) #}
      <input class="form-control" id="motCle" name="motCle" value="{{ modele.mot_cle }}">
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
        <option value="">(tous)</option>
        {% for genre in modele.genres %}
        {# selected: a Boolean attribute, set if the condition is true, omitted otherwise #}
        <option value="{{ genre }}"{{ " selected" if genre == modele.genre }}>{{ genre }}</option>
        {% endfor %}
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Rechercher</button>
    </div>
  </form>
  <p>{{ modele.resultats | length }} livre(s) trouvé(s).</p>
  <ul>
    {% for livre in modele.resultats %}
    <li><i>{{ livre.titre }}</i>, {{ livre.auteur }} ({{ livre.genre }})</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}
  • line 6: the [<form>] tag. The [action] attribute is the URL to which the form is submitted; [method="get"] places the fields in the URL. The classes in [Bootstrap] arrange the fields on a single line;
  • Line 8: a label. Its attribute [for] specifies the identifier ([id]) of the field it describes: clicking on the label places the cursor in the field, and screen readers read the label along with the field;
  • Line 10: an input field. Its attribute [name] is the name of the parameter sent to the server: this is the link between the form and the action ([request.args.get("motCle")]). The attribute [value] is the displayed value: the previous entry, redisplayed (and escaped by [{{ }}], which is essential in an attribute: an entry containing a quotation mark ["] would otherwise close the attribute);
  • lines 14–20: a drop-down list. Each [<option>] has a value ([value]), sent to the server, and text, displayed. The first option, with an empty value, means “all genres”;
  • line 18: the option selected in the previous request is assigned the attribute [selected]. This is a Boolean attribute: its presence alone is sufficient; it has no value. The conditional expression without [else] determines whether or not it is written;
  • line 23: the submit button ([type="submit"]);
  • line 26: the number of results.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form Fields
docs.text:
Manually entering the HTML for each field, re-displaying its value, checking the correct boxes, and selecting the correct options is repetitive work and prone to errors. The [WTForms] library does this for us. A form is described there by a class, where each attribute is a field; each field knows how to:

  • how to bind to the query: read its value from the submitted data and convert it to its type;
  • validate itself, based on its list of validators (Example 19);
  • display itself in HTML, along with its current value.

The [Flask-WTF] extension integrates [WTForms] into [Flask]: its forms read the current request themselves, and they are protected against CSRF attacks (we’ll get to that). This example shows all the field types in a HTML form.

docs.title: 4.6.1. The lists service: services/listes.py
docs.text:
# services/listes.py: the lists provided by the form. In a real
# application, they would come from a database: they would be read UNE times
# at startup, since they are the same for all users.
from flask import current_app


class ListesService:

     # Each list: pairs (sent value, displayed text)
    def titres(self) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        return [(t, t) for t in ("Mr", "Mme", "Melle")]

    def pays(self) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        return [("fr", "France"), ("be", "Belgique"), ("ch", "Suisse"), ("ca", "Canada")]

    def loisirs(self) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        return [(l, l) for l in ("lecture", "musique", "sport", "cinéma")]

    def langues(self) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
        return [(l, l) for l in ("français", "anglais", "espagnol", "allemand")]


def listes_service() -> ListesService:
    return current_app.extensions["listes"]

The form’s dropdown lists (titles, countries, hobbies, languages) are provided by a service, following the model in Example 06: in a real application, they would come from a database. Each option is a pair [(valeur, texte)]: the value sent to the server and the text displayed. [[(t, t) for t in (...)]] creates pairs where both elements are identical. The function [listes_service] makes the object unique, stored in [app.extensions] by [app.py]:

# app.py: the application from Example 18
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask

from controllers.formulaire import formulaire
from services.listes import ListesService

# Bootstrap, shared across the examples (see Example 15)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
     # the application’s secret key: it signs the forms’ anti-CSRF token
     # (see models/saisie.py). In production, a long random string, kept secret
    app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "une-cle-secrete-pour-l-exemple-18"
     # the list service: a single, shared object (see Example 06)
    app.extensions["listes"] = ListesService()
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(formulaire)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • line 19: [app.config] is the application configuration, a dictionary. The key [SECRET_KEY] is the application’s secret key: [Flask] and its extensions use it to sign data entrusted to the browser—that is, to add a digital fingerprint that only the key’s holder can calculate. Any modification of the data by the browser is thus detected. [Flask-WTF] needs it for its anti-CSRF tokens; we’ll see it again in the session cookie (example 20). In production, it’s a long random string that must never appear in the source code (the chapter on authentication will read it from an environment variable);
  • Line 21: The single service shared by all requests.

docs.title: 4.6.2. The form: models/saisie.py
docs.text:
# models/saisie.py: the form, described by a class WTForms. Each field
# can be read from the request (binding) and displayed in HTML (rendering)
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import (DateField, HiddenField, PasswordField, RadioField,
                     SelectField, SelectMultipleField, StringField, TextAreaField)
from wtforms.validators import Optional
from wtforms.widgets import CheckboxInput, ListWidget

from services.listes import listes_service


# checkboxes: a multiple-choice list (SelectMultipleField),
# displayed as a list of checkboxes (widgets) instead of a drop-down list
class CasesACocher(SelectMultipleField):
    widget = ListWidget(prefix_label=False)
    option_widget = CheckboxInput()


# FlaskForm: a WTForms form adapted for Flask; it reads the fields itself
# from the current POST request, and contains a hidden field [csrf_token]
class SaisieForm(FlaskForm):
    jeton = HiddenField()
    titre = RadioField("Titre")
    nom = StringField("Nom")
    mot_de_passe = PasswordField("Mot de passe")
     # an <input type="date"> field exchanges its values in the yyyy-mm-dd format;
     # Optional: the field may remain empty
    naissance = DateField("Date de naissance", validators=[Optional()])
    loisirs = CasesACocher("Loisirs")
    pays = SelectField("Pays")
    langues = SelectMultipleField("Langues parlées")
    commentaire = TextAreaField("Commentaire")

     # drop-down lists, provided by the service each time the form is created
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        listes = listes_service()
        self.titre.choices = listes.titres()
        self.pays.choices = listes.pays()
        self.loisirs.choices = listes.loisirs()
        self.langues.choices = listes.langues()
  • Lines 14–16: [WTForms] does not have a “checkboxes” field. However, a group of checkboxes with the same name is, for the server, a multiple-choice list: it sends zero, one, or more values. We therefore create a class derived from [SelectMultipleField] that changes only its presentation: a field’s widget is the object that generates its HTML; [ListWidget] renders a list of options, and each option is rendered by [CheckboxInput], a checkbox;
  • line 21: the form inherits from [FlaskForm], the base class of [Flask-WTF];
  • lines 22–32: the fields. The first parameter is the label. Each field class corresponds to a HTML element:
Field WTFormsHTML element generated[StringField][<input type="text">][PasswordField][<input type="password">], never pre-filled[HiddenField][<input type="hidden">], an invisible field[DateField][<input type="date">], whose value is converted to [date][IntegerField], [EmailField][<input type="number">], [<input type="email">] (example 19)[RadioField]a group of radio buttons: a single value[SelectField]a drop-down list [<select>]: a single value[SelectMultipleField]a list [<select multiple>]: multiple values[TextAreaField]a text box [<textarea>], multi-line[BooleanField]a single checkbox, converted to a Boolean
  • Line 28: The validator [Optional()] allows the field to remain empty (otherwise, converting an empty string to a date would fail). A field [<input type="date">] exchanges its values with the server in the format [aaaa-mm-jj], regardless of the format in which the browser displays it;
  • lines 35–41: dropdown fields require their list of options ([choices]). This list is provided each time the form is created, in the constructor, via the [__init__] method. It first calls the parent class’s constructor ([super().__init__(...)]), passing it all its parameters, and then populates the fields. A field [titre] declared at the class level becomes, within the object, a linked field ([self.titre]) specific to this form.

docs.title: 4.6.3. The controller: controllers/formulaire.py
docs.text:
# controllers/formulaire.py: a form that uses all field types
from flask import Blueprint, render_template, request

from models.saisie import SaisieForm

formulaire = Blueprint("formulaire", __name__, url_prefix="/formulaire")


# GET: the form, with initial values (named parameters: one per field)
@formulaire.get("")
def afficher():
    form = SaisieForm(titre="Mme", pays="fr", langues=["français"], jeton="A7X2")
    return render_template("formulaire/formulaire.html", form=form)


# POST: SaisieForm() reads the submitted fields; the form displays them again
@formulaire.post("")
def traiter():
    form = SaisieForm()
     # validates: checks the anti-CSRF token and the field constraints
    valide = form.validate()
     # what the browser actually sent, parameter by parameter
    recu = "\n".join(f"{nom} = [{', '.join(valeurs)}]"
                     for nom, valeurs in request.form.lists())
    return render_template("formulaire/formulaire.html", form=form, recu=recu,
                           valide=valide)
  • line 12: A form created during a request (GET) does not read anything: its fields take the values passed to the constructor (named parameters, one per field) or remain empty. These are the form’s initial values;
  • line 13: the form itself is passed to the view, which will render it;
  • line 19: During a POST request, [FlaskForm] reads the submitted fields ([request.form]) itself: each field takes the received value, converted to its type;
  • line 21: [validate()] runs the validators for each field and returns [True] if all are satisfied. Dropdown fields automatically verify that the received value is among their options: a malicious user can send anything, not just what the page offered. [Flask-WTF] adds an anti-CSRF token check to this;
  • Lines 23–24: For the example, the list of what the browser actually sent: [request.form.lists()] returns, for each parameter, its name and the list of its values. [", ".join(...)] combines them into a single string.

docs.title: 4.6.4. The view: templates/form/formulaire.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Un formulaire complet</h1>
  <form method="post" action="/formulaire" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# hidden fields: the Flask-WTF anti-CSRF token and our field [jeton] #}
    {{ form.csrf_token }}
    {{ form.jeton }}

    <div class="mb-2">
      <span class="form-label me-3">{{ form.titre.label.text }}</span>
      {# radio buttons: we iterate through the field’s options; same as [name], a single value is sent #}
      {% for option in form.titre %}
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        {{ option(class="form-check-input") }}
        {{ option.label(class="form-check-label") }}
      </div>
      {% endfor %}
    </div>

    <div class="row g-2 mb-2">
      <div class="col">
        {# A field is displayed as APPELANT; its parameters become attributes HTML #}
        {{ form.nom.label(class="form-label") }}
        {{ form.nom(class="form-control") }}
      </div>
      <div class="col">
        {# A password is not returned to the page: JAMAIS omits it #}
        {{ form.mot_de_passe.label(class="form-label") }}
        {{ form.mot_de_passe(class="form-control") }}
      </div>
      <div class="col">
        {{ form.naissance.label(class="form-label") }}
        {{ form.naissance(class="form-control") }}
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="mb-2">
      <span class="form-label me-3">{{ form.loisirs.label.text }}</span>
      {# Checkboxes: same as [name], multiple values possible #}
      {% for option in form.loisirs %}
      <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
        {{ option(class="form-check-input") }}
        {{ option.label(class="form-check-label") }}
      </div>
      {% endfor %}
    </div>

    <div class="row g-2 mb-2">
      <div class="col">
        {{ form.pays.label(class="form-label") }}
        {{ form.pays(class="form-select") }}
      </div>
      <div class="col">
        {{ form.langues.label(class="form-label") }}
        {# multiple-select list: multiple values possible #}
        {{ form.langues(class="form-select", size=4) }}
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="mb-2">
      {{ form.commentaire.label(class="form-label") }}
      {# text field: the value is ENTRE the tags #}
      {{ form.commentaire(class="form-control", rows=2) }}
    </div>

    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Envoyer</button>
  </form>

  {% if recu is defined %}
    <h2 class="h5 mt-3">Ce que le serveur a reçu</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">{{ recu }}</pre>
    <p>Formulaire valide : {{ "oui" if valide else "non" }}</p>
    {# form.errors: a field-to-list dictionary of its error messages #}
    <ul>
      {% for champ, messages in form.errors.items() %}
      <li>{{ champ }} : {{ messages | join(", ") }}</li>
      {% endfor %}
    </ul>
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 5: a form POST;
  • line 7: the hidden field containing the anti-CSRF token. A CSRF attack (*Cross-Site Request Forgery*) involves a malicious site tricking the victim’s browser into sending a form to our application. The browser includes our application’s cookies in the request—and thus the logged-in user’s session—so the request appears legitimate. The defense: every form in our application contains a random token linked to the user’s session and signed with the secret key, which the malicious site cannot know. [Flask-WTF] rejects any POST form whose token is missing or invalid;
  • line 8: a field is rendered by calling it, or simply by inserting it into the page via [{{ }}] (which is equivalent to calling it without parameters). The HTML it produces is not escaped: [WTForms] marks it as safe (the values it places in it are, however, escaped);
  • Lines 13–18: a group of radio buttons. Iterated through by a loop, the field renders its options, one per button: each is drawn ([option(...)]) and has its own label ([option.label(...)]). All radio buttons share the same attribute, [name]: only one is selected at a time, and only one value is submitted;
  • lines 24–25: the label and the input field. The named parameters of the call become attributes HTML: [class="form-control"]. Since the term [class] is reserved in [Python], [WTForms] also accepts [class_];
  • line 30: [PasswordField] never redisplays the received value: a password should not be sent back and forth within a HTML page;
  • Lines 41–46: Checkboxes, styled the same way as radio buttons. They also have the same [name]; however, multiple checkboxes can be selected, and the browser then sends multiple values (e.g., 10);
  • line 57: the multi-select list, displayed across four lines ([size]);
  • line 64: the text field, spanning two lines;
  • lines 70–80: the condition [is defined] is true if the variable [recu] has been passed to the view (via the action POST). [form.errors] is a dictionary that associates each invalid field with a list of its error messages; [items()] returns these pairs. The filter [join] combines the elements of a list.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text: A registration form, where each field has its own constraints. If an error occurs, the form is redisplayed with the user’s input and a message below each field containing an error.

docs.title: 4.7.1. The form: models/inscription.py
docs.text:
# models/inscription.py: the form fields and their constraints
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import EmailField, IntegerField, PasswordField, StringField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, Email, EqualTo, InputRequired, Length, NumberRange


# a FILTRE: it transforms the received value AVANT for validation;
# Here, the spaces surrounding the input are removed
def nettoyer(valeur):
    return valeur.strip() if isinstance(valeur, str) else valeur


class InscriptionForm(FlaskForm):

     # the language of the messages that WTForms writes itself (conversion impossible,
     # for example: “abc” in an integer field)
    class Meta:
        locales = ["fr"]

     # Each field: a label, filters, and a list of validators, each
     # with its own error message. DataRequired rejects an empty entry (or one containing
     # of spaces); it also generates the attribute HTML5 [required]
    nom = StringField("Nom", filters=[nettoyer], validators=[
        DataRequired("Le nom est obligatoire."),
        Length(max=20, message="Le nom ne doit pas dépasser 20 caractères.")])

     # EmailField: an <input type="email"> field
    email = EmailField("Adresse électronique", filters=[nettoyer], validators=[
        DataRequired("L'adresse électronique est obligatoire."),
        Email("Adresse électronique invalide.")])

     # anything coming from a form is a string: IntegerField converts it
     # ("42" -> 42); InputRequired: the input must not be empty
    age = IntegerField("Âge", validators=[
        InputRequired("L'âge est obligatoire."),
        NumberRange(min=18, max=120, message="L'âge doit être compris entre 18 et 120 ans.")])

    mot_de_passe = PasswordField("Mot de passe", validators=[
        DataRequired("Le mot de passe est obligatoire."),
        Length(min=6, message="Le mot de passe doit comporter au moins 6 caractères.")])

     # a rule that applies to DEUX fields: EqualTo compares this field to another
    confirmation = PasswordField("Confirmation", validators=[
        DataRequired("La confirmation est obligatoire."),
        EqualTo("mot_de_passe", message="La confirmation ne correspond pas au mot de passe.")])
  • Lines 9–10: A [WTForms] filter is a function that transforms the received value before validation. It removes the spaces surrounding a string (an input such as [" "] becomes empty and will be rejected by [DataRequired]). The [isinstance] test protects against a missing value ([None]);
  • lines 17–18: the internal class [Meta] controls the form’s behavior. [locales = ["fr"]]: The messages that [WTForms] generates itself (an impossible conversion, an invalid selection, etc.) will be in French; [WTForms] comes with their translations. [app.py] disables the translation mechanism of [Flask-WTF] ([WTF_I18N_ENABLED = False]) for this purpose; otherwise, it would wait for the [Flask-Babel] extension;
  • lines 23–25: The parameter [validators] is the list of field validators, executed in order. Each receives its own error message. [DataRequired] rejects an empty value; [Length] limits the length of the string;
  • lines 28–30: [EmailField] generates a [<input type="email">]; the validator [Email] checks the address syntax (using the library [email-validator], already used by [Pydantic] in Example 08);
  • lines 34–36: [IntegerField] converts the entire input. [InputRequired] requires an input; unlike [DataRequired], it checks that something has been entered, rather than whether the converted value is “true”: [DataRequired] would reject an age of 0, because [0] is false in [Python]. [NumberRange] limits the value;
  • Lines 43–45: a rule that applies to two fields: [EqualTo("mot_de_passe")] compares the value of one field to that of another field.

Validators are also used for display purposes: [WTForms] derives attributes from HTML5 ([required], [maxlength], [minlength], [min], [max]), which allow the browser to verify the input even before it is submitted (we’ll cover this later). A “custom” validator is a function that takes the form and the field as arguments and raises a [ValidationError] (from the [wtforms.validators] module) if the value is invalid; it can also be written as a form method named [validate_<champ>]. [WTForms] provides other ready-to-use validators: [Regexp] (a regular expression), [AnyOf] (a list of allowed values), [Optional]... The case study uses these.

docs.text:
# controllers/inscription.py: a form validated by the server
from flask import Blueprint, render_template, request

from models.inscription import InscriptionForm

inscription = Blueprint("inscription", __name__, url_prefix="/inscription")


# ?html5=true: the browser is allowed to validate the form before submission
def html5_demande() -> bool:
    return request.args.get("html5") == "true"


@inscription.get("")
def afficher():
    return render_template("inscription/inscription.html", form=InscriptionForm(),
                           html5=html5_demande())


@inscription.post("")
def inscrire():
    form = InscriptionForm()
     # validate_on_submit: the request is a POST ET—the form is valid
    if not form.validate_on_submit():
         # The form is RÉAFFICHE: entered values (except passwords),
         # and a message below each invalid field (see fragments/champ.html)
        return render_template("inscription/inscription.html", form=form,
                               html5=html5_demande(),
                               erreur="Le formulaire contient des erreurs.")
    return render_template("inscription/bienvenue.html", form=form)
  • lines 10–11: the parameter [?html5=true] enables browser-side validation (see below);
  • line 24: [validate_on_submit()] returns [True] if the request is a POST and if the form is valid;
  • Lines 27–29: The invalid form is redisplayed: it is the same [form] object, which contains the user’s input and the errors for each field. The variable [erreur] is a general message displayed at the bottom of the page by the template;
  • line 30: the valid form—the welcome page. (The following example will show that it is better to redirect after a successful POST.)

docs.title: 4.7.3. A reusable field: templates/fragments/champ.html
docs.text:
Each field is displayed in the same way: a label, the input field, and, in case of an error, the area outlined in red and the message below it. A macro prevents having to write this five times:

{# an input field, with its label and its PREMIER error message.
   field.errors : la liste des messages d'erreur du champ ; les attributs HTML5
   (required, maxlength, minlength, min, max) sont écrits par WTForms lui-même,
   d'après les validateurs du champ #}
{% macro champ(field) %}
<div class="mb-2">
  {{ field.label(class="form-label") }}
  {{ field(class="form-control" ~ (" is-invalid" if field.errors else "")) }}
  {% if field.errors %}
  <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ field.errors[0] }}</div>
  {% endif %}
</div>
{% endmacro %}
  • line 5: the macro receives a field from the form;
  • line 8: the class [is-invalid], derived from [Bootstrap], frames the field in red. It is added if the field’s error list, [field.errors], is not empty;
  • Lines 9–11: The first error message for the field, in a [invalid-feedback] element, which [Bootstrap] displays in red below a [is-invalid] field.

docs.title: 4.7.5. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s submit a form full of errors: a name consisting of spaces, an address without a full domain, an age of 12, a password that’s too short, and a different confirmation:

The input was preserved (except for the passwords), and each error is flagged below its corresponding field. With [curl], this time providing the anti-CSRF token, we can also submit something a browser wouldn’t send—a non-numeric age: the conversion message, generated by [WTForms], is in French thanks to [locales]:

  <input class="form-control is-invalid" id="age" max="120" min="18" name="age" required type="number" value="abc">
  <div class="invalid-feedback">N' is not a valid integer.</div>

We can also see the HTML5 attributes inferred from the validators: [required], [min], [max].

docs.title: 4.7.6. Browser validation
docs.text:
Let’s remove the [novalidate] attribute by clicking the “Enable” link (parameter [?html5=true]). The browser then checks the attributes [required], [type="email"], [min], [maxlength]... itself before submitting the form, and displays its own messages:

This validation is convenient for the user: it’s immediate, with no back-and-forth with the server. But it does not replace server-side validation: a user can disable it, and a program like [curl] ignores it completely. The rule is absolute: the server always validates; browser-side validation is merely an added convenience.

A correct entry, at last. The name, entered with spaces on either side, was cleaned up by the filter:

docs.title: 4.8. Example 20: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
When a POST action responds with a page, that page is the result of a POST. If the user reloads the page (presses [F5]), the browser sends the POST request, after displaying a warning that few people read: the command is sent twice, and the message is posted twice. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern (PRG) avoids this problem: a successful POST action does not return a page; it responds with a redirect (example 04) to a page GET, which the browser requests immediately. Reloading this page simply re-executes the GET action.

There is still one problem: the page GET wants to display a message (“the task has been added”), but it is the action POST that knows this message, and it cannot pass a variable to a request that has not yet occurred. The solution: a flash message, posted by the POST action, retained until the next request, displayed, and then discarded.

docs.title: 4.8.1. The service: services/taches.py
docs.text:
# services/taches.py: the list of tasks, in memory, shared by all
from threading import Lock

from flask import current_app


class TachesService:

    def __init__(self):
        self._taches = ["Lire le chapitre 3"]
         # Multiple requests may run (EN, MÊME, TEMPS; the server
         # processes them on multiple threads): a lock ensures that only one
         # thread at a time reads or modifies the list
        self._verrou = Lock()

    def liste(self) -> list[str]:
        with self._verrou:
            return list(self._taches)  # a COPIE: the caller cannot modify ours

    def ajouter(self, libelle: str):
        with self._verrou:
            self._taches.append(libelle)


def taches_service() -> TachesService:
    return current_app.extensions["taches"]
  • Line 14: The task list is shared by all requests. However, the development server processes each request on a different thread: two requests can run at the same time and modify the list simultaneously. A lock ([Lock], from the standard module [threading]) ensures that only one thread at a time executes the code it protects. The prefix [_] indicates, by convention, an internal attribute of the class;
  • line 17: the statement [with] acquires the lock, executes the block, and then releases the lock, even if the block throws an exception. A thread that finds the lock acquired waits until it is released;
  • line 18: the method returns a copy of the list: the caller can safely iterate over it while another thread adds a task to the original.

docs.title: 4.8.2. The controller: controllers/taches.py
docs.text:
# controllers/taches.py: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern
from flask import Blueprint, flash, redirect, render_template, request, url_for

from services.taches import taches_service

taches = Blueprint("taches", __name__, url_prefix="/taches")


# GET /tasks: the list and the add form
@taches.get("")
def afficher():
    return render_template("taches/taches.html", taches=taches_service().liste())


# POST /tasks: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern
@taches.post("")
def ajouter():
    libelle = request.form.get("libelle", "")
    texte = libelle.strip()
    if not texte or len(texte) > 40:
         # Invalid input: the page is reloaded without redirection
        return render_template("taches/taches.html", taches=taches_service().liste(),
                               libelle=libelle,
                               erreur="Le libellé doit comporter de 1 à 40 caractères.")
    taches_service().ajouter(texte)
     # A "flash" message: it will persist through the redirect for the request SUIVANTE
    flash(f"La tâche [{texte}] a été ajoutée.")
     # No page: a redirect to the page GET
    return redirect(url_for("taches.afficher"))


# POST /tasks/no-program: the counterexample (a page in response to POST)
@taches.post("/sans-prg")
def ajouter_sans_prg():
    libelle = request.form.get("libelle", "").strip()
    taches_service().ajouter(libelle or "(sans titre)")
    return render_template("taches/taches.html", taches=taches_service().liste(),
                           sans_prg=True)
  • lines 18–24: The input is validated manually, without [WTForms], to keep the example simple. An invalid entry is redisplayed without redirection: there is nothing to protect against a duplicate submission, since nothing has been modified;
  • line 27: [flash] sets a message for the next request;
  • line 29: the redirect to the GET page;
  • lines 34–38: the counterexample: a page in response to POST.

docs.title: 4.8.4. Where are flash messages stored?
docs.text:
Between the POST request and the subsequent GET request, the message must be stored somewhere. [Flask] stores it in the user’s session (see the chapter on scopes). By default, the session for [Flask] is not stored on the server: it is stored in a cookie sent to the browser, which resends it with every request. To prevent the user from tampering with it, the cookie is signed with the secret key—which is why [app.py] sets it. Let’s examine this using [curl]. The [-c] option logs the received cookies to a file, while the [-b] option returns those from the file:

curl -i -c cookies.txt -d "libelle=Faire%20les%20exercices" http://localhost:5000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 201
Location: /taches
Set-Cookie: session=.eJyrVopPy0kszkgtVrKKrlZSKAFSSrmpxcWJ6alKOko-iQolMaUGBqlGyRmpCtFuiZlFqQo5qcUKqRWpRcmZyanFsQqJCmAVlhCFlgqJWfmlUHaqnlJsbWwtAJ5zIV4.arfJyw.XBeb5pAbuGT1H1-IhwuRM6NVuro; HttpOnly; Path=/
...

The response to POST is a redirect (status code 302, header [Location]), accompanied by a cookie [session]. Its value consists of three parts, separated by periods: the data, compressed and Base64-encoded; the signature date; and the signature. When decoded, the data is readable:

{"_flashes":[{" t":["message","La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée."]}]}

The session for an application named [Flask] is therefore readable by the user (it is not encrypted), but tamper-proof (it is signed): nothing secret is stored in it. The attribute [HttpOnly] prevents the [JavaScript] on the page from reading the cookie. Let’s follow the redirect by sending the cookie back:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt http://localhost:5000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 916
Set-Cookie: session=; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; HttpOnly; Path=/
...
    <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée.</div>
    <main>
  <h1 class="h3">Mes tâches</h1>
  <ol>
    <li>Lire le chapitre 3</li>
    <li>Faire les exercices</li>
  </ol>
...

The message is displayed, and the session—now empty—is deleted: the server returns an empty cookie whose expiration date has passed. A new request for GET would no longer display the message.

docs.text:
Adding a task: the browser followed the redirect; the URL is the one for the GET page, which can be safely reloaded.

An invalid entry, redisplayed with its error message:

The counterexample: the page is the response to POST, and its URL is [/taches/sans-prg]. If you click on [F5], the browser asks if you want to resubmit the form; if you agree, the task is added a second time.

docs.title: 4.9. Example 21: Links, Buttons, and Confirmation
docs.text:
A principle of the HTTP protocol: a GET request does not change anything. Browsers, search engines, and tools that preload pages freely follow links without asking the user for permission. A “delete” link ([<a href="/contacts/2/supprimer">]) would therefore be dangerous: a bot crawling the site would delete everything. In a web application:

  • viewing is done via a link ([<a href>]), which sends a GET request;
  • editing (save, duplicate, delete) is done via a button placed in a form (POST), protected by an anti-CSRF token.

This example manages a list of contacts and displays a confirmation window before each deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.1. The service: services/contacts.py
docs.text:
# services/contacts.py: contacts, stored in memory, shared by everyone
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from threading import Lock

from flask import current_app


# a contact: an ID, a name, a phone number
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Contact:
    id: int
    nom: str
    telephone: str


class ContactsService:

    def __init__(self):
        self._contacts = [
            Contact(1, "Marie Durand", "01 23 45 67 89"),
            Contact(2, "Paul Martin", "06 12 34 56 78"),
            Contact(3, "Philippe Jandot", "02 98 76 54 32"),
        ]
        self._dernier_id = 3
        self._verrou = Lock()

    def liste(self) -> list[Contact]:
        with self._verrou:
            return list(self._contacts)

     # the contact, or None if it does not exist
    def lire(self, id: int) -> Contact | None:
        with self._verrou:
            return next((c for c in self._contacts if c.id == id), None)

    def modifier(self, id: int, nom: str, telephone: str) -> Contact | None:
        with self._verrou:
            for i, contact in enumerate(self._contacts):
                if contact.id == id:
                     # A contact is immutable (frozen): creates a new one
                     # new one, which replaces the old one in the list
                    self._contacts[i] = replace(contact, nom=nom, telephone=telephone)
                    return self._contacts[i]
            return None

    def ajouter(self, nom: str, telephone: str) -> Contact:
        with self._verrou:
            self._dernier_id += 1
            contact = Contact(self._dernier_id, nom, telephone)
            self._contacts.append(contact)
            return contact

    def supprimer(self, id: int) -> Contact | None:
        with self._verrou:
            contact = next((c for c in self._contacts if c.id == id), None)
            if contact is not None:
                self._contacts.remove(contact)
            return contact


def contacts_service() -> ContactsService:
    return current_app.extensions["contacts"]

An in-memory service, protected by a lock like the one in Example 20. A few points about [Python]:

  • line 34: the expression in parentheses is a generator (see Example 05) of contacts whose ID matches the one being searched for; [next] returns the first element, or the default value [None] if none exists;
  • line 38: [enumerate] iterates through a list, returning the index and the element for each item;
  • line 42: A contact is immutable ([frozen=True]); the function [replace] in the module [dataclasses] creates a copy of it, with certain attributes changed;
  • The methods return [None] for a nonexistent contact: it is up to the controller to decide on the response.

docs.title: 4.9.2. The controller: controllers/contacts.py
docs.text:
# controllers/contacts.py: links (GET) and buttons (POST)
from flask import Blueprint, abort, flash, redirect, render_template, request, url_for

from services.contacts import contacts_service

contacts = Blueprint("contacts", __name__, url_prefix="/contacts")


# the contact, or a 404 response if it does not exist
def contact_ou_404(contact):
    if contact is None:
        abort(404, "contact inconnu")
    return contact


# a LIEN (<a href>): a GET request, which does not change anything
@contacts.get("")
def liste():
    return render_template("contacts/liste.html", contacts=contacts_service().liste())


@contacts.get("/<int:id>")
def fiche(id):
    contact = contact_ou_404(contacts_service().lire(id))
    return render_template("contacts/fiche.html", contact=contact)


# a BOUTON in a POST form: a request that modifies data
@contacts.post("/<int:id>")
def enregistrer(id):
    contact = contact_ou_404(contacts_service().modifier(
        id, request.form.get("nom", ""), request.form.get("telephone", "")))
    flash(f"Le contact [{contact.nom}] a été modifié.")
    return redirect(url_for("contacts.liste"))


# same form, different button (formaction attribute): different action
@contacts.post("/<int:id>/dupliquer")
def dupliquer(id):
    copie = contacts_service().ajouter(request.form.get("nom", "") + " (copie)",
                                       request.form.get("telephone", ""))
    flash(f"Le contact [{copie.nom}] a été créé.")
    return redirect(url_for("contacts.liste"))


@contacts.post("/<int:id>/supprimer")
def supprimer(id):
    contact = contact_ou_404(contacts_service().supprimer(id))
    flash(f"Le contact [{contact.nom}] a été supprimé.")
    return redirect(url_for("contacts.liste"))
  • lines 10–13: a utility function: a nonexistent contact stops the action with a 404 response;
  • lines 17–23: the two actions GET, which do not modify anything: the list and a contact’s record;
  • lines 29–34: saving the record: an action POST, which follows the pattern PRG. The same URL and [/contacts/2] are handled by two different actions, depending on the method: GET displays, POST saves;
  • Lines 38–43: duplication—another action, POST, triggered by a second button on the same form;
  • lines 46–50: deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.3. Anti-CSRF protection: app.py
docs.text:
# app.py: the application from Example 21
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Blueprint, Flask

from flask_wtf.csrf import CSRFProtect

from controllers.contacts import contacts
from services.contacts import ContactsService

# Bootstrap, shared across the examples (see Example 15)
BOOTSTRAP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "commun" / "bootstrap"


def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.jinja_env.trim_blocks = True
    app.jinja_env.lstrip_blocks = True
    app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "une-cle-secrete-pour-l-exemple-21"
    app.extensions["contacts"] = ContactsService()
    app.register_blueprint(Blueprint("bootstrap", __name__, static_folder=BOOTSTRAP,
                                     static_url_path="/bootstrap"))
    app.register_blueprint(contacts)
     # Flask-WTF’s anti-CSRF protection, for TOUTES the requests POST from
     # the application: each form must return the token csrf_token()
    CSRFProtect(app)
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    create_app().run(port=5000, debug=True)
  • line 26: In examples 18 and 19, it was the [WTForms] form that verified its token, in [validate()]. Here, the forms are written by hand, without [WTForms]. [CSRFProtect] extends protection to the entire application: before each request (POST, as well as PUT, PATCH, DELETE), it verifies the token and returns a 400 status code if it is missing or invalid, even before the action is called. An action cannot omit it. This is the configuration that the case study will use.

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Contacts</h1>
  <table class="table align-middle">
    <tbody>
      {% for contact in contacts %}
      <tr>
        <td>{{ contact.nom }}</td>
        <td>{{ contact.telephone }}</td>
        <td class="text-end">
          {# view: a simple link; url_for places the ID in the path: /contacts/2 #}
          <a class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" href="{{ url_for('contacts.fiche', id=contact.id) }}">Voir</a>
          {# Delete: a form POST, the submission of which will be confirmed #}
          <form method="post" class="d-inline" action="{{ url_for('contacts.supprimer', id=contact.id) }}"
                data-confirmation="Supprimer le contact {{ contact.nom }} ?">
            {# the anti-CSRF token, required by CSRFProtect (see app.py) #}
            <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token() }}">
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" type="submit">Supprimer</button>
          </form>
        </td>
      </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 13: a link, presented as a button by the classes of [Bootstrap] ([btn]...): the appearance has nothing to do with the HTTP method. [url_for('contacts.fiche', id=contact.id)] places the ID in the path: [/contacts/2];
  • lines 15–20: a POST form for each “Delete” button, with no fields other than the token. The [d-inline] class displays it on the same line as the link. The [data-confirmation] attribute contains the confirmation message: the [data-...] attributes are unassigned, intended for the [JavaScript] on the page;
  • Line 18: The function [csrf_token()], provided to the views by [Flask-WTF], returns the session's anti-CSRF token; it is placed in a hidden field named [csrf_token].
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Contact n° {{ contact.id }}</h1>

    <button class="btn btn-outline-primary" type="submit"
            formaction="{{ url_for('contacts.dupliquer', id=contact.id) }}">Dupliquer</button>

docs.title: 4.9.5. The confirmation window
docs.text:
The browser can display a confirmation box (function [JavaScript] [confirm]), but it is not very attractive, and its appearance depends on the browser. Here we use a modal window from [Bootstrap], displayed by a few lines of [JavaScript]. The window is a fragment included in the template and is therefore present—though hidden—on all pages:

{# a single window for the entire page, hidden (d-none) by default #}
<div id="modale-confirmation" class="d-none">
  <div class="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
  <div class="modal fade show d-block" tabindex="-1" role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true">
    <div class="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
      <div class="modal-content">
        <div class="modal-header">
          <h5 class="modal-title">Confirmation</h5>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-body">
          <p class="mb-0" id="modale-confirmation-message"></p>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-footer">
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary" data-action="non">Non, revenir</button>
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-danger" data-action="oui">Oui, confirmer</button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 2: the [d-none] class from [Bootstrap] hides the element;
  • lines 3–4: the gray background, followed by the window, are rendered by the classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 11: the message's position;
  • lines 14–15: the two buttons, of type [button] (not [submit]: they do not submit any form), distinguished by their [data-action] attribute.
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Contacts</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('bootstrap.static', filename='css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {% for message in get_flashed_messages() %}
    <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">{{ message }}</div>
    {% endfor %}
    <main>
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
  </div>
  {# the confirmation window, present on all pages #}
  {% include "fragments/confirmation.html" %}
  {# the script, at the bottom of the page: the elements it looks for already exist #}
  <script src="{{ url_for('static', filename='js/app.js') }}"></script>
</body>
</html>
  • line 19: the window, included on all pages;
  • line 21: the script, placed at the end of the page: when it runs, the elements it searches for already exist.

The [static/js/app.js] script:

// Confirmation for forms with the data-confirmation="..." attribute
// Without JavaScript, these forms are simply submitted without confirmation.
(() => {
  const modale = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation');
  const message = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation-message');
  let enAttente = null; // The form to submit if confirmation is given

   // 1. We intercept the submission of forms requiring confirmation
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((formulaire) => {
    formulaire.addEventListener('submit', (evenement) => {
      evenement.preventDefault(); // The submission is suspended
      enAttente = formulaire;
      message.textContent = formulaire.dataset.confirmation;
      modale.classList.remove('d-none'); // the window appears
    });
  });

   // 2. The two buttons in the window
  modale.addEventListener('click', (evenement) => {
    const action = evenement.target.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'oui') {
      enAttente.submit(); // Submit, SANS Trigger the 'submit' event again
    } else if (action === 'non') {
      modale.classList.add('d-none');
      enAttente = null;
    }
  });
})();
  • line 3: the code is enclosed in an anonymous function, which is executed immediately; its variables do not interfere with those of the other scripts on the page;
  • lines 4–6: the window, the message location, and the form awaiting confirmation;
  • lines 9–14: for each form that has a [data-confirmation] attribute, the [submit] event—triggered when the form is submitted—is intercepted. [preventDefault()] suspends submission; the form is put on hold, and its message ([dataset.confirmation], the value of the [data-confirmation] attribute) is displayed in the window, which appears;
  • lines 19–25: a single handler for clicks in the window: [evenement.target] is the element clicked; its attribute [data-action] specifies which button it is. “Yes” submits the pending form using the [submit()] method, which—unlike clicking a button—does not trigger the [submit] event (otherwise, the window would reappear); “No” hides the window.

Without [JavaScript], the form is simply submitted without confirmation: the page remains usable. This is progressive enhancement: [JavaScript] adds convenience, but the application does not depend on it.
